Stay vigilant, and prioritize security in every layer of your infrastructure.

item.title: Radio With No Radar: Why Agent Runtime Security Fails Without the Layers Beneath It
item.description: On The Hacker News: Runtime enforcement in agentic AI systems is more than a technical challenge—it's a governance imperative. Visibility into agents’ behavior, connections, and permissions is critical. Without it, even well-intentioned tools can bypass controls and expose data. The recent case where an AI assistant routed emails through a personal account highlights how runtime rules must block risky actions in real time. Yet, most solutions ignore the reality that agents operate within third-party platforms, making traditional gateways ineffective. The inspection point for agent traffic isn’t always where the enterprise expects. Platforms like Salesforce, Slack, and Microsoft 365 host agents that run within their trust boundaries. This means security teams can’t rely on a single gateway to monitor all activity. The OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 calls this the “unreachable skill” scenario. The lesson from past security shifts—like moving from network to application-layer inspection—applies here. Agent runtime needs a similar move, but with added complexity: the application layer belongs to someone else. A runtime strategy must span multiple vantage points, not just a single gateway. Enforcement needs a live map of identity, permissions, and activity to judge gray cases accurately. A millisecond verdict requires context—like the agent’s owner, the data’s sensitivity, and the delegation chain. Without this, security becomes reactive, not proactive. Mature enforcement allows known-good actions, warns on plausible risks, and blocks hostile chains. It also logs every decision with a full causal path, which is essential for incident reviews and regulatory compliance. The end-state fallacy is a common mistake. Assuming inline enforcement will see everything overlooks the need for foundational layers like discovery, posture, and identity. What’s available now is the stack runtime depends on. Vendors that built for the problem can answer key questions about how they manage agent discovery, governance, and enforcement. Platforms like Reco offer a holistic view by connecting all identities, applications, and permissions into a single live map. This approach transforms reach into the unit of analysis, not configuration.

item.title: Docker Sandboxes vulnerability lets AI agents access sensitive files outside their sandbox (CVE-2026-103916)
item.description: On Endor Labs: The Docker Sandboxes vulnerability (CVE-2026-103916) highlights a critical flaw in how AI agents interact with file systems. The sbx cp command bypasses the allowlist, allowing agents to access or overwrite files outside their sandbox. This is a direct risk to data integrity and confidentiality. It underscores the need for stronger sandbox controls and careful handling of file operations. The vulnerability exploits symbolic links, enabling agents to trick the CLI into copying files beyond the intended scope. This means an attacker could inject malicious code or steal sensitive data through a prompt injection attack. The implications are severe, especially in agentic workflows where agents often propose copy commands. Operators must remain vigilant and verify paths before executing any file transfer. Docker's fix, delayed until version 0.51.0, shows how complex these security boundaries can be. Until then, treat sbx cp like any untrusted command. Resolve paths manually, confirm they stay within approved directories, and be wary of copy operations the agent suggests. This is a reminder that isolation is only as strong as the controls that enforce it. This isn't the first time such a flaw has emerged. It reinforces the need for rigorous model evaluation and monitoring. AI agents operate in environments where trust is paramount, and any gap in containment can lead to serious breaches. As we build more agentic systems, we must ensure every channel is secured, not just the obvious ones.

item.title: Binance details recruiter impersonation behind $6.3B wallet breach
item.description: On TechTarget: Binance’s $6.3 billion breach highlights how developer access can become a security liability. Attackers used fake job interviews and a compromised coding assignment to infiltrate systems. The malware in the assignment bypassed endpoint defenses and exploited internal AI tools. This underscores the need for strict controls on what developers can download and execute on corporate laptops. Developer environments are inherently risky. They require downloading packages and running code, which complicates endpoint security. Organizations must enforce limits on execution permissions and what can be introduced into development systems. Without these controls, a single compromised device can escalate into a full-scale breach. Social engineering tactics like recruiter impersonation exploit trust in recruitment processes. Attackers used fabricated HR and CEO personas to gain access to sensitive information. Security teams must treat recruitment outreach to engineers as part of the attack surface. Interview code should never run on production systems or devices with privileged access. This incident reinforces the importance of balancing developer needs with security. Controls must prevent unauthorized code execution and limit permissions without hindering productivity. Organizations must assume developers will interact with external tools and enforce strict governance around those interactions.

item.title: What CISOs should know about SaaS security in the age of AI
item.description: On TechTarget: SaaS security is evolving rapidly with the integration of AI. The old questions about access and configuration still matter but now carry new weight. AI agents can act on behalf of users in ways that expand risk exposure. A simple CRM access might now mean an agent can process thousands of records across multiple systems. This changes the potential impact of excessive privilege. The visibility challenge is also growing. Vendors often add AI features through updates, blurring the line between approved SaaS and approved AI. Security teams must now inventory not just applications, but also embedded AI, models, and nonhuman identities. These elements create new attack surfaces that traditional tools may not cover. AI introduces risks like nonhuman identities, over-permissioning, and prompt injection. Agents often inherit user privileges, which is convenient but dangerous. A compromised agent can escalate access quickly. Prompt injection can manipulate AI into exposing data or triggering unintended actions. These issues demand a shift in how we govern and monitor AI-enabled SaaS. CISOs need to extend existing governance models to cover AI in SaaS. Every AI-enabled offering should have clear ownership, data classification, and permission controls. Visibility into agent behavior and data flow is critical. By applying familiar security principles to AI systems, we can manage risk without stifling innovation.

item.title: AI threats create urgent need to renew cybersecurity information-sharing law, businesses tell Congress
item.description: On Cybersecurity Dive: The reauthorization of CISA 2015 is more than a legislative formality. It’s a critical enabler for the rapid, secure exchange of threat intelligence in an era where AI is accelerating both attack surfaces and response times. The law’s liability protections have been a cornerstone for public-private collaboration, especially in regulated industries where compliance and risk management are paramount. Urgent action is needed as the law faces expiration. Without legal certainty, the pace of information sharing could slow, leaving critical infrastructure vulnerable. The recent vulnerability crises underscore how essential timely intelligence is. AI-driven threats demand a framework that supports machine-speed collaboration without compromising security or regulatory requirements. The House’s NDAA draft includes a reauthorization provision, but the Senate’s version omits it. This divergence highlights the need for consensus. As we approach the reconciliation phase, it’s vital that lawmakers recognize the role of CISA 2015 in enabling the agility required to defend against modern cyber threats. The stakes are too high for half-measures. The speed and breadth of threat intelligence sharing define our ability to keep pace with adversaries. CISA 2015 provides that legal certainty. Its reauthorization is a necessary step in strengthening our collective defense.

item.title: LLMjacking Emerges as Thriving Cybercriminal Enterprise
item.description: On Dark Reading: LLMjacking has evolved into a serious threat, with cybercriminals reselling cloud access to large language models as a profitable venture. The financial impact on victims can be staggering, with some organizations facing bills exceeding $1 million before access is revoked. This underscores the need for stronger identity and access management practices. The attack vectors often involve stolen or exposed credentials, such as IAM tokens or service account keys. Attackers may operate quietly, using minimal API requests to validate access without triggering alerts. This stealthy approach allows them to monetize stolen access before detection. Defenders must focus on early detection of compromised identities and unauthorized access. Implementing centralized secrets management, least privilege access, and continuous monitoring can help identify and mitigate these threats before they escalate. The rise of LLMjacking highlights the importance of credential hygiene and IAM best practices. Organizations must treat these areas with the same rigor as traditional cybersecurity threats. Proactive defense is critical in an environment where AI models are increasingly targeted.

item.title: Binance Reveals How Fake Job Interviews and AI Tool Abuse Led to $6.43 Billion Theft
item.description: On The Hacker News: Binance's $6.43 billion theft was the result of a multi-stage attack that began with a compromised developer environment. The threat actor used a trojanized Homebrew installer to gain initial access, highlighting the risks of untrusted software in supply chain attacks. This underscores the need for strict control over developer tools and environments. The attack escalated through social engineering, with fake job interviews used to compromise two engineers. The threat actor leveraged internal AI tools to move laterally within the network, demonstrating how internal systems can become critical attack vectors if not properly secured. This is a stark reminder of the importance of AI governance and tooling security. Binance's response included rebuilding systems, enhancing security controls, and improving detection mechanisms. The incident shows that no organization is immune to sophisticated attacks, especially when multiple vectors are exploited. Proactive defense and continuous monitoring are essential in today's threat landscape. The attack also revealed how North Korean threat actors refine their techniques through smaller breaches before targeting larger organizations. This highlights the need for a layered security approach that includes both technical and human factors. We must stay vigilant and adapt our defenses to evolving threats.

item.title: The Blind Spot in the SDLC: Who, and What, Is Acting on Your Code?
item.description: On Blueflagsecurity: The SDLC is more than just code. It's a pipeline of identities, tools, and processes that move software from idea to production. The blind spot isn't in the code itself—it's in who and what is acting on it. Attackers are exploiting identities, not vulnerabilities. Stolen CI tokens, service accounts, and even AI coding agents are becoming the entry point for breaches. These identities often have access to critical systems and code, yet they're rarely reviewed or monitored. AI coding agents are rewriting the rules. They can write, review, and merge code with no human oversight. Many operate under administrator accounts with no one watching. As their use grows, so does the risk of uncontrolled code flow and credential theft. The solutions are clear. But the challenge is visibility. Without connecting the dots between identities, tools, and pipelines, we can't stop breaches in progress. It's time to rethink how we secure the SDLC.

item.title: PHP2Shell and AI Put Half the Internet on Edge
item.description: On IEEE Spectrum: The PHP2Shell vulnerability exposed a critical flaw in legacy systems, highlighting how decades-old code can be weaponized in new ways. AI tools are now helping researchers uncover these hidden risks faster than ever before. This isn’t just about finding bugs—it’s about understanding how to exploit them in ways humans alone might miss. The out-of-memory error in PHP, long dismissed as a minor crash, became a major threat when combined with AI’s ability to simulate complex reasoning. This shows how technical debt in legacy software is now being paid with new tools that can turn theoretical risks into real-world exploits. Formal verification and AI-generated patches are emerging as critical defenses. While LLMs can draft fixes and even prove their correctness, human oversight remains essential. The goal is to make patching as automated as discovery, but trust must be earned through rigorous validation. This is a wake-up call for all of us. Legacy systems are still the backbone of critical infrastructure, and AI is now both a weapon and a shield. Proactive governance, continuous monitoring, and formal verification must become standard practice.

item.title: Storm Ransomware Is Scaling Fast and Selling an AI Powered Image
item.description: On Checkpoint: Storm's AI branding, despite lacking concrete evidence, highlights a growing trend where cybercriminals use AI narratives to recruit and build brand identity. This mirrors how legitimate enterprises leverage AI for innovation and differentiation. For security leaders, it underscores the need to monitor not just the technology but the messaging around it. The AI claim appears closely tied to recruitment and marketing, not operational capabilities. Storm's structured affiliate model and polished leak site suggest a focus on scale and visibility rather than AI-driven attacks. This shift reflects a broader move toward branding in cybercrime, where perception can drive growth. As defenders, we must adapt by scrutinizing both the tools and the narratives. AI security isn't just about protecting models—it's about understanding how adversaries use technology to gain trust and scale. This requires a dual focus on technical defenses and strategic awareness.

item.title: Shutting the Door on the XCPE Botnet | Google Cloud Blog
item.description: On Cloud google: The XCPE botnet incident underscores a critical flaw in supply chain security. A major OEM preloaded malicious code into millions of devices, enabling ad fraud, data exfiltration, and proxy networks. This wasn’t an isolated incident but a deliberate monetization strategy. The malware bypassed firmware checks by loading after first boot. This highlights the need for stronger firmware integrity controls. OEMs and cloud providers must collaborate to close these gaps. Google’s response—banning Videostrong and enhancing review processes—shows the importance of proactive measures. But lasting change requires ongoing disruption of these interconnected ecosystems. This case isn’t just about malware. It’s about trust. Users shouldn’t be unknowingly used as distribution channels. We must prioritize transparency and security at every layer.

item.title: As the White House touts its AI task force, CISA is conspicuously missing
item.description: On Cybersecurity Dive: The White House’s new AI task force has sparked debate over its approach to cybersecurity. While the initiative aims to address AI’s risks, it has notably excluded CISA, an agency with deep expertise in critical infrastructure protection and incident response. This omission could lead to redundant guidelines and confusion for businesses navigating AI security challenges. CISA’s role in safeguarding infrastructure is critical, yet its absence from the task force raises concerns about the effectiveness of the guidance being developed. U.S. cybersecurity experts warn that without CISA’s involvement, the task force may produce half-baked policies that fail to address the complex interplay between AI and digital threats. CISA’s experience in managing incident reporting and fostering collaboration with private-sector operators is unmatched. Their work on the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) and AI-specific guidance demonstrates their readiness to contribute meaningfully to the task force’s goals. The task force’s success hinges on the quality of its advisory network. CISA’s relationships with infrastructure operators and its understanding of AI’s risks and opportunities position it as the ideal partner. Excluding CISA risks creating silos and duplicating efforts, ultimately undermining the trust and collaboration needed to secure the nation’s digital future. It’s time for the task force to recognize the value of CISA’s expertise and integrate it into their strategy.

item.title: Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses Key Detail
item.description: On Dark Reading: Microsoft's dominance in the public sector means its legacy software remains a critical part of the attack surface. With an 85% market share, Microsoft's products are prime targets for nation-state actors seeking access to sensitive government data. This creates a disproportionate risk, as Microsoft accounts for nearly 16% of known exploited vulnerabilities this year — the highest among all vendors. The report highlights government agencies as primary targets but misses the broader impact of legacy software on security. Vendors must prioritize security before release, even if it slows feature development. Customers should demand more transparency and accountability from their suppliers to mitigate risks. Microsoft's recent Patch Tuesday disclosed 974 vulnerabilities, likely aided by AI. Yet this is not enough. The threat landscape is evolving rapidly, and AI is being used by attackers to launch more sophisticated campaigns. Nation-state actors are leveraging AI to scale and enhance their operations, making the need for stronger vendor security more urgent than ever. The VA's experience with a Microsoft monoculture serves as a cautionary tale. Relying on a single vendor increases exposure and limits options. As AI tools become more advanced, the stakes will only rise. Vendors must take responsibility for security, and customers must hold them accountable. Otherwise, the threat environment will continue to worsen.

item.title: Binance Hack: One Compromised Laptop Can Cost Billions in Crypto
item.description: On Dark Reading: The Binance breach is a stark reminder of how a single compromised device can lead to systemic loss. A developer's laptop became the entry point for attackers who exploited internal systems to drain billions. This highlights the need for layered, independent controls to prevent a single breach from escalating into a catastrophic event. The incident underscores the importance of segregation between critical systems and everyday operations. Developers and admins should have isolated workstations to limit the impact of a compromised endpoint. 24/7 monitoring and anomaly detection are also essential to catch suspicious activity early. Organizations must test attack paths and assume that no single control is enough. The Binance breach shows how attackers can bypass normal approval processes using internal signing systems. Security needs to shift from verifying identity to governing the consequences of actions. This isn't just a crypto issue. Any enterprise with critical systems and privileged access must ask: what stops an attacker after initial access? The answer lies in containment, layered defenses, and continuous testing of all possible attack routes.

item.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
item.description: On Krebsonsecurity: Google and industry partners dismantled a botnet using 1.3 million Android TV boxes as proxies. The malware, named XCPE, secretly rented users' internet connections for malicious activities like ad fraud. This highlights the risks of compromised IoT devices and the need for stronger manufacturer accountability. The botnet’s reach extended beyond TV boxes to other IoT products like healthcare devices and karaoke machines. This underscores the importance of collaboration between industry players to secure the supply chain and prevent such large-scale compromises. Manufacturers must prioritize security from the start. Google’s actions show that even with security tests, vulnerabilities can be exploited. It’s a wake-up call for the industry to enforce stricter standards and hold manufacturers responsible for their products’ security. This incident is a clear example of how insecure IoT devices can be weaponized. We need stronger regulations, better transparency, and more shared responsibility to protect users from these kinds of threats.

item.title: PEDM vs. Standing Elevated Privileges: Control Access Without Flooding the Helpdesk
item.description: On The Hacker News: Privilege elevation and delegation management (PEDM) offers a smarter way to control access without flooding the helpdesk. Instead of granting standing elevated privileges, PEDM elevates specific actions for a defined time and under strict rules. This approach reduces the attack surface by limiting elevated access to only what's needed, aligning with Zero Trust principles. It ensures that privileges exist only when a legitimate action requires them, not as a default for users or systems. Standing privileges create unnecessary exposure. Local admin rights, broad server access, or shared accounts often remain active long after their initial purpose. This leaves endpoints vulnerable if compromised, allowing attackers to move laterally or disable controls. PEDM addresses this by separating the task from the user, focusing on the action rather than the person. This granular control improves security without disrupting workflows. Implementing PEDM requires understanding what work truly needs elevation. Start by mapping user workflows and identifying trusted actions. Define rules around specific applications, commands, or scripts, not just user roles. Use attributes like file hashes or digital signatures to narrow scope. This precision prevents over-privileged access while ensuring critical tasks can still run smoothly. PEDM is not a set-and-forget solution. Regularly review exceptions, refine rules, and adjust policies based on real-world usage. Start small, test with a representative group, and define an emergency path to maintain operations without abandoning security. The goal is to create a policy that reflects how your organization actually works, not a static list of exceptions.

item.title: Is Your SOC Ready for AI Agents? A Maturity Check Before You Deploy
item.description: On The Hacker News: AI SOC agents are redefining how we handle alerts. They start at the bottom layer, alert handling, and return analyst hours that let teams work on layers above. If your MDR flags threats too slowly or hands back alerts without context, these agents can bridge the gap. They pull context from your systems and record evidence behind each conclusion, letting your team verify the work. A SOC needs more than just the right tools. It needs data access, context, and written standards. AI agents can only investigate what they can query. If they can't access your SIEM or identity provider, they miss key details. Readiness means API access, asset context, and healthy data pipelines. A quick test: list the queries a senior analyst ran to close five recent incidents. Any query the agent can't run is a gap to fix before a pilot. Define what a complete investigation looks like and record your baseline. A written standard helps grade the agent's performance. Keep a list of detections turned off due to capacity issues. When an agent investigates every alert, some of those rules can come back. Track metrics like share of alerts investigated, mean time to investigate, and how often closed alerts are reopened. The survey shows an average of 75 minutes for a thorough investigation, but alerts often wait close to an hour before being opened. If your SOC struggles with delayed escalations, lack of context, or closed alerts without explanation, AI agents are a fit. But readiness depends on data access, written standards, and defined permissions. Start with read-only access for investigations, then widen permissions as confidence grows. The same rules apply as for a new human analyst. A ready SOC has these rules written down before a pilot starts.

item.title: Critical Langflow Flaws Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Run Code on Servers
item.description: On The Hacker News: Langflow's recent vulnerabilities highlight a critical risk for enterprise security. The flaws allow unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication or execute code on servers, which is alarming for any organization using this platform. These vulnerabilities span multiple versions, emphasizing the urgency of patching. The implications are significant, especially in environments where AI orchestration is central to operations. The unauthenticated remote code execution flaw is particularly concerning. It leverages the Model Context Protocol to expose tools, potentially enabling attackers to interact with the system without credentials. This underscores the need for strict access controls and continuous monitoring. Enterprises must ensure their systems are not only patched but also configured to mitigate such risks. Upgrading to version 1.13.0 is essential, but the process requires careful planning. Backing up data and preparing for password sign-in are critical steps. Organizations should also evaluate their current deployment and consider alternative solutions if immediate upgrades are not feasible. The stakes are high, and the consequences of inaction could be severe.

item.title: CVE-2026-98432: Reported AI-Built Remote Root Exploit Precedes Distribution Fixes
item.description: On Cloud Security Alliance Labs: The AI-generated exploit for CVE-2026-98432 highlights a growing risk: malicious models can now turn theoretical vulnerabilities into real-world threats. This remote root chain, reported by Anthropic, shows how AI can bypass KASLR and execute arbitrary code with minimal timing precision. The flaw exists in core IPv4 TCP code and has been around since 2016, yet patching lagged for months. The gap between upstream fixes and distribution updates is alarming. While the kernel fix was available by October 5, major distros like RHEL and Ubuntu had no patches as late as October 30. This delay leaves systems exposed to AI-driven exploitation, especially when combined with MPTCP or Go-based services. Default settings in Go 1.24 and Linux kernels can unintentionally expose attack vectors. Organizations must act fast. Prioritize patching Linux hosts accepting untrusted IPv4 TCP traffic. Use vendor security trackers, not version strings, to assess status. Apply live patches where available, and disable MPTCP where unnecessary. Go services should set GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 to mitigate risk, but this is a temporary fix until the kernel is patched. This case underscores the need for proactive AI security. Traditional patch management is no longer enough. Teams must assume that exploit diffs will be analyzed by automated systems. Rethink severity triage—complex races may be trivial for AI. Align with vendors that offer live patches and track exposure-based remediation. The patch debt crisis is real, and AI is accelerating it.

item.title: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer
item.description: On Cisco Talos: VOLTA is a Windows infostealer that leverages LLMs to prioritize victims after stealing credentials. It builds a structured bundle of data and sends it to an LLM for monetization ranking. This shifts the post-theft analysis to an AI model, acting as an intelligence analyst for the attacker. The malware uses a multi-model architecture to handle refusals, falling back to a chain of models if needed. This resilience suggests the operator expects model guardrails and wants reliable output. The prompt emphasizes accuracy and specific inferences from sparse data. The integration of AI in malware isn’t about speed but effort displacement. It reduces the need for manual analysis, allowing attackers to focus on other tasks. This trend highlights the growing role of AI in cybercrime and the need for stronger governance and monitoring.

item.title: Postgres 19 is late, and it's AI's fault
item.description: On Rhaas blogspot: PostgreSQL 19 is late and it’s AI’s fault. The delay isn’t due to a lack of effort but rather the sheer volume of bugs being uncovered by LLMs. These models are now finding issues in legacy systems like PostgreSQL that humans missed for decades. The result is more back-patch commits and a slower release cycle. The project’s commitment to quality is evident. While LLMs help identify bugs faster, they still require human review. This means more work for developers, but also a higher standard of code. The shift is clear: AI is raising the bar for software security and reliability. For teams building with LLMs, this means greater responsibility. AI can draft fixes, but final validation remains a human task. Developers must ensure their code meets standards and is secure. The challenge is to adapt quickly while maintaining trust in the systems we build. The long-term impact is uncertain. With decades of hidden bugs now exposed, how do we keep innovating? It’s a critical question for the future of software. One thing is clear: AI is changing how we approach security, compliance, and quality.

item.title: Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks
item.description: On Dark Reading: Legacy software can be a silent threat. When apps are abandoned, their infrastructure often remains active, creating supply chain vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit. The recent case of Time4Popcorn, a BitTorrent client from 2014, shows how outdated domains can be hijacked by malicious actors. Over 2.5 million machines still check these domains, offering a backdoor for exploitation. This isn't just about old code. It's about the persistence of infrastructure that was never properly decommissioned. Attackers can register these domains and inject malicious updates, bypassing security measures. The rise of AI makes this even more dangerous, as it enables faster discovery and exploitation of these weaknesses. Dropcatch domains are a growing risk. They're often integrated into software supply chains, allowing threat actors to launch sophisticated attacks. With AI, the barrier to entry for these attacks is dropping. Defenders must stay ahead by identifying and securing unused infrastructure before it's too late. Organizations need to understand the domains their systems rely on. Remote work and BYOD have expanded attack surfaces, making visibility and control more critical than ever. Collaboration and proactive defense are essential to disrupt these schemes and protect the supply chain.

item.title: VAPOR PANDA Uses AI-Driven ARTEX to Grow Global Espionage Campaign
item.description: On CrowdStrike: CrowdStrike recently uncovered a VAPOR PANDA campaign using ARTEX to execute multi-target intrusions globally. The adversary leveraged AI-driven frameworks to scale operations across 200+ organizations in 14 countries. This marks a shift from single-target attacks to parallel, automated engagements. The use of ARTEX with DeepSeek and a commercial LLM highlights how adversaries are combining open-source tools with commercial models to build scalable, persistent threats. The operation revealed a sophisticated blend of agentic workflows and traditional tradecraft. Attackers used AI to coordinate tasks, evade sensors, and exploit multiple attack paths simultaneously. This includes leveraging cloud services, Active Directory, and network infrastructure to maintain access. The integration of sensor evasion directly into the agentic process shows a growing sophistication in how threats are structured and executed. This campaign underscores the need for advanced detection and response strategies. Traditional methods are no longer sufficient against AI-powered, multi-agent intrusions. Organizations must adopt real-time EDR solutions, enforce strict access controls, and monitor for ARTEX-specific indicators. The rise of agentic frameworks like ARTEX demands a proactive approach to AI security and threat modeling. We must stay ahead of these evolving tactics to protect critical assets.

item.title: Trojanized Claude Code Extension Plants an SSH Backdoor
item.description: On Opensourcemalware: The supply chain is a critical attack surface, and this incident shows how dangerous it can be when trusted tools are compromised. A malicious version of the Claude Code extension in the Cursor Marketplace was published, embedding a persistent SSH backdoor. The malicious code runs before the legitimate extension, allowing attackers to install an authorized SSH key and establish a reverse tunnel. This gives them remote access to the host and the ability to exfiltrate data. The attack leverages the trust developers place in their tools. Extensions are often auto-updated, making them a prime vector for compromise. The malicious version was disguised as a legitimate release, and its code was prepended to the normal bundle. This makes detection harder, as the extension appears normal but behaves differently at runtime. It also suppresses errors to avoid triggering alerts. This incident underscores the need for rigorous vetting of third-party extensions and the risks of relying on marketplaces to validate publisher identities. A package claiming to be from a trusted source isn’t necessarily authorized by that source. The responsibility lies with the marketplace to ensure authenticity. Developers and organizations must demand transparency and verify the integrity of all tools they use.

item.title: Trojanized Claude Code Extension Delivered Persistent SSH Backdoor to Developer Machines
item.description: On Stepsecurity: The incident around the Claude Code extension highlights a critical vulnerability in supply chain trust. A malicious loader was embedded in a legitimate VS Code extension, granting attackers persistent SSH access to developer machines. This underscores the need for rigorous vetting of third-party tools and extensions. The attack leveraged a tampered extension distributed through Cursor's marketplace, embedding a loader that silently implants SSH keys and establishes reverse tunnels. The loader’s simplicity and lack of obfuscation make it a stark reminder of how easily trusted software can be weaponized. Monitoring for unexpected changes in trusted software is non-negotiable. Developers and security teams must implement strict version control, source verification, and real-time telemetry to detect anomalies. The incident also reinforces the importance of zero-trust principles in modern infrastructure. This isn’t just about extensions—it’s about the broader ecosystem of tools we rely on. We must build resilience into our processes and tools, ensuring that trust is never assumed but always validated.

item.title: In the wild: Trojanized Claude Code extension opening SSH tunnels on developer Macs
item.description: On Daylight: The article highlights a trojanized Claude Code extension that silently installs a reverse SSH tunnel on developer Macs. The implant leverages trusted IDE tools to execute malicious behavior without user interaction. It plants an SSH key, creates a fake Apple service, and opens a backdoor to an attacker’s server. This underscores the risks of relying on third-party extensions in development environments. The attack chain is subtle. It uses legitimate processes and files to mask its presence, making it hard to detect. Aura’s investigation showed the malware was already active on developer machines before public disclosure. This emphasizes how quickly such threats can spread and how critical rapid response is in AI-driven workflows. Governance and control are non-negotiable in agentic AI and multi-agent orchestration. Tools like Cursor extensions must be rigorously audited for unintended behavior. We need stronger telemetry, real-time monitoring, and strict access controls to prevent weaponization of trusted tools. The line between helpful AI and malicious code is thin. This incident is a wake-up call. Developers and security teams must treat all AI-driven tools with the same scrutiny as traditional software. We need to build systems that can detect and respond to anomalous behavior in real time. The future of security lies in proactive, intelligent defense that understands the intent behind every action.

item.title: Official Claude Code Extension Compromise: Security Advisory
item.description: On Phorion: Phorion recently uncovered a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace. The compromised bundle drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This is a clear example of how supply chain risks can escalate in regulated environments. Third-party tools must be vetted with strict governance and continuous monitoring. The malware attempts to enable SSH on macOS but fails due to a logic flaw. It checks the Remote Login state without elevation and misinterprets the error as "SSH is already on." This oversight means the backdoor doesn’t activate if SSH isn’t already running. Still, it installs persistence and beaconing capabilities, making it a serious threat. Organisations should audit their environments for use of the affected extension versions. Even if the SSH setup fails, the persistence and reconnaissance features remain active. This incident underscores the need for rigorous third-party tool vetting and real-time monitoring. It’s not enough to rely on static checks—dynamic behavior must be observed. The malware installs a LaunchAgent to survive reboots and sets up a reverse SSH tunnel to an external server. It collects host data and sends it back to the attacker. This highlights how supply chain compromises can lead to long-term access. Teams must ensure their tools are secure from the start.

item.title: Inside a malicious Claude Code-branded extension and its persistent SSH backdoor
item.description: On Microsoft: The supply chain attack via a malicious Claude Code-branded extension highlights the critical need for strict control over extension publishers. Attackers leveraged the Cursor marketplace to deploy a persistent SSH backdoor, underscoring how trusted platforms can become vectors for compromise. Organizations must enforce publisher verification and restrict access to approved sources. Monitoring for unusual SSH activity is essential in detecting such threats. The loader attempted to establish reverse SSH tunnels, plant keys, and configure persistence across multiple platforms. Even if access wasn’t achieved, the presence of these artifacts indicates a breach. Teams should review telemetry for signs of unauthorized SSH connections or modified configuration files. This incident reinforces the value of proactive defense. Immediate actions include hunting for the malicious extension, checking for unauthorized SSH keys, and removing persistence artifacts. It’s also vital to rotate credentials and isolate affected systems. Regular audits and strict control over extension deployment can mitigate similar risks.

item.title: No quarantine for Bedrock Mantle
item.description: On Plerion: The AWS quarantine policy for Bedrock-Mantle is missing a critical piece. It denies bedrock:InvokeModel but leaves bedrock-mantle:CreateInference open, creating a gap that could enable LLMjacking. This is a clear oversight in a landscape where agentic AI systems require proactive governance. The issue isn’t just about access control. Without logging, you can’t detect or respond to misuse. Mantle inference calls are data events, but they’re off by default and often ignored. This means you’re blind to what’s happening in your environment. If you’re running agentic AI, you need visibility. Enable CloudTrail data events for AWS::BedrockMantle::Project to track inference activity. Or, if you don’t need the service, deny it entirely. Don’t wait for AWS to catch up.

item.title: Manifestos, Fear, and ‘Loser Thinking’: Inside Proton’s AI Reckoning
item.description: On 404media: Proton's AI push shows a clear tension between speed and security. The CEO's emphasis on velocity over caution raises concerns about how quickly the company is adopting AI without proper governance. This approach risks undermining the very privacy and security principles Proton is known for. The culture inside Proton appears to prioritize AI adoption over critical feedback. Employees describe an environment where dissent is discouraged, and concerns about security are often silenced. This creates a disconnect between the company's public mission and its internal practices. Rapid AI deployment without adequate testing or oversight can lead to vulnerabilities that compromise user trust. Proton’s focus on revenue growth over security alignment highlights the need for a balanced approach that doesn’t sacrifice compliance for speed. As leaders, we must ensure that AI adoption doesn’t come at the cost of governance. Speed shouldn’t mean skipping security checks or ignoring regulatory requirements. The right balance is essential for long-term trust and compliance.

item.title: Building Trusted AI Infrastructure
item.description: On Eclypsium: NVIDIA and Eclypsium are setting a new standard for securing agentic AI infrastructure. Their collaboration combines NVIDIA BlueField’s hardware-rooted trust with Eclypsium’s Infrastructure Assurance to create a verifiable chain of trust. This is critical as AI agents grow more autonomous and interact with sensitive data across systems. BlueField DPUs provide a secure foundation by running critical services independently of host workloads. This separation enables distinct trust domains, allowing operators to manage and protect infrastructure without relying on application-level controls. It’s a key part of securing agentic AI, where independent verification and enforcement are essential. Eclypsium enhances this by offering continuous monitoring, firmware integrity checks, and configuration assessment. Together, they ensure that infrastructure remains in a known-good state and detect unauthorized changes or persistent threats. This approach aligns with my focus on Zero Trust and AI governance, emphasizing verifiable trust over assumed trust. Building trusted AI requires more than just secure models. It demands infrastructure that can independently observe, enforce policies, and maintain security across the entire stack. NVIDIA and Eclypsium’s work shows how hardware and software can work together to achieve this, supporting the evolving needs of agentic AI systems.

item.title: Cloud CISO Perspectives: Introducing new $250,000 tier for Google Cloud VRP (Q&A) | Google Cloud Blog
item.description: On Cloud google: The new $250,000 Root-in-Cloud tier for Google Cloud VRP signals a shift in how we value and incentivize high-impact security research. It’s designed to reward human-led discovery of complex architectural flaws that require deep systems analysis and agentic tools. This tier acknowledges the growing role of agentic AI in uncovering vulnerabilities that automated methods alone cannot detect. The program’s emphasis on proof-of-root and cryptographic validation ensures researchers can test without compromising production environments. This approach balances innovation with safety, allowing the community to explore new attack vectors while maintaining strict boundaries. It’s a clear step toward safer, more transparent research practices. For enterprise CISOs, this means preparing for agent-generated submissions and accelerating remediation timelines. With automation reducing the time between disclosure and exploitation, defensive strategies must evolve. Prioritizing coordinated disclosure and maintaining high standards for security partners are critical to mitigating risks in this new era. The rise of agentic tools is reshaping the security landscape. While they empower researchers, they also introduce new governance challenges. CISOs must lead by example, fostering a culture of responsible disclosure and ensuring that speed never comes at the cost of user safety. The future of security depends on balancing innovation with accountability.

item.title: Prediction Markets Emerge as a New Vertical for Traffer Teams
item.description: On Recordedfuture: Prediction markets are becoming a new playground for fraud teams, leveraging AI to create convincing platforms that mimic legitimate services. These scams use AI to automate content creation, social engineering, and victim engagement, making it easier than ever to scale fraudulent operations. The result is a dangerous blend of financial speculation and exploitation, where victims are tricked into depositing funds under the guise of trading. The threat is real and evolving. Fraud actors are now using AI to generate synthetic influencers, craft deceptive promotional content, and even simulate trading activity to build trust. This level of sophistication means we must rethink our defenses. Traditional security measures are no longer sufficient to detect or prevent these advanced scams. We need stronger AI governance frameworks and robust detection mechanisms that can identify and neutralize these threats before they scale. This includes monitoring for AI-generated content, enhancing model evaluation processes, and implementing real-time anomaly detection for financial transactions. The goal is to stay ahead of bad actors who are constantly adapting their tactics. Without proactive measures, we risk allowing these scams to proliferate. It's time to prioritize AI security and model monitoring as critical components of our overall cybersecurity strategy. Let's build systems that are not only secure but also capable of defending against the next wave of digital threats.

item.title: A Defense Contractor Gave Their Personal AI Agent Access to a Secure Pentagon System
item.description: On Wired: A contractor connected a secure Pentagon system to their personal AI agent, exposing sensitive data and login credentials to a third-party site. This highlights the risks of personal AI agents accessing secure environments. The incident shows how even unclassified information can become a national security threat when mishandled. The breach wasn’t reported quickly, reflecting broader governance issues in handling AI in sensitive contexts. Contractors often face conflicting priorities between speed and security. This case shows how AI can bypass traditional controls, creating new vulnerabilities that are hard to detect. AI agents can automate tasks but also exfiltrate data unnoticed. The lack of oversight and clear policies around AI use in regulated environments leaves systems exposed. This incident underscores the need for stronger governance, transparency, and accountability in AI deployment.

item.title: Security notice — malicious version of Anthropic.claude-code (2.1.312 and 2.1.313) identified in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace · Cursor
item.description: On Cursor: The recent incident with the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace highlights the critical need for rigorous vetting of third-party extensions. A malicious version of the Anthropic.claude-code extension was distributed, embedding a backdoor that attempts to establish a persistent SSH tunnel. This underscores the risks of untrusted extension ecosystems, especially in enterprise environments where security is paramount. The attack collects system details and tries to install an SSH backdoor, though it fails without admin rights on most systems. The persistence mechanisms and unauthorized SSH keys are still present, making it essential to validate installations and check for the svc-telemetry key. This is a stark reminder of the hidden dangers in seemingly benign tools. Remediation steps include running validation scripts, isolating affected hosts, and removing the malicious key and persistence scripts. It’s crucial to rotate credentials and assess the need for system rebuilds. This incident reinforces the importance of continuous monitoring and strict access controls in securing development environments.

item.title: Security Logging in Cloud Environments - Kubernetes
item.description: On Marcolancini: The importance of comprehensive logging in Kubernetes environments cannot be overstated. With workloads running in ephemeral clusters, traditional cloud logs often stop at the edge of the control plane. This leaves critical security events—like kubectl exec sessions or secret reads—unlogged. Tools like Falco or Tetragon can bridge this gap by capturing runtime events that escape the API layer. These sensors watch system calls and provide visibility into actions that don’t touch the API server. Runtime sensors are essential for detecting anomalies that go unnoticed by audit logs. They track activities inside containers, such as shell access or unauthorized file reads. On managed platforms like EKS or GKE, enabling these sensors is straightforward, but custom rules for specific workloads may require additional tools. The choice between Falco and Tetragon often comes down to the level of control and the types of events you need to monitor. Both offer valuable insights, though their approaches differ in how they interact with the kernel. Even with all logs enabled, blind spots remain. For example, direct kubelet API calls bypass the API server entirely, making them invisible to standard logging. Similarly, non-standard pods and containers—like static or init containers—can evade detection by tools that rely solely on the API. These gaps highlight the need for a layered approach, combining audit logs, control plane metrics, and runtime sensors to ensure no event goes unrecorded. The goal is to create a complete picture of cluster activity that supports fast, accurate incident response.

item.title: UK to look at making software companies liable for cyber breaches
item.description: On Therecord: The UK government is moving toward holding software companies accountable for cyber breaches, a shift that could redefine how tech vendors approach security. This proposal, outlined in budget documents, aims to address the growing economic and national security risks posed by insecure products. The move reflects increasing pressure from cybersecurity authorities to enforce stronger standards, especially after high-profile incidents like the Jaguar Land Rover breach. The consultation will explore liability frameworks, potentially expanding the PSTI Act to cover software and AI systems. This aligns with broader European efforts, such as the Cyber Resilience Act, which imposes strict penalties for insecure products. However, challenges remain, including defining responsibility and ensuring compatibility with EU regulations to avoid duplication for businesses. For organizations in regulated sectors, this signals a need to proactively embed security and compliance into product development. As AI and agentic systems become more prevalent, governance frameworks must evolve to manage risks and ensure accountability. The UK’s approach could set a precedent for other markets seeking to balance innovation with responsibility.

item.title: A Shared Language for Agent Defense: Introducing Project Quarry
item.description: On Blogs cisco: Project Quarry marks a pivotal step in securing agentic AI. Traditional defenses struggle with multi-step attacks that blend permitted actions into harmful sequences. Quarry offers a detection language that captures these patterns, enabling security teams to spot threats in agent behavior across time and context. It's not just about individual actions but how they connect to form risk. This approach mirrors how fraud detection systems track purchase patterns. A single step might seem harmless, but the sequence can signal a breach. Quarry brings this same level of pattern recognition to agent activity, combining neural and symbolic checks for a comprehensive view. It's designed to work with the full trace of an agent’s actions, not just isolated events. For regulated environments, this is critical. Compliance frameworks like HIPAA and HITRUST demand visibility into how systems operate. Quarry supports this by preserving session history and providing evidence for each finding. It also integrates with AI security frameworks, translating risk categories into actionable rules that can be tested and refined. Quarry isn’t a replacement for authorization controls or content classifiers. It complements them by identifying suspicious sequences that individual actions might miss. The language is open, allowing teams to test, share, and extend it. This collaborative approach ensures the community can address emerging risks faster than any single product could.

item.title: n0n Ransomware: Inside an AI-Assisted Extortion Operation
item.description: On Socradar: n0n ransomware represents a new threat vector in cybersecurity. This group leverages AI to automate extortion, using tools like opencode to generate attack scripts. The operator spent over $7,000 on LLM API usage, highlighting the growing role of AI in cybercrime. The group’s modus operandi relies on stolen credentials, not exploits. They exfiltrate data and destroy it, often leaving victims with no backups. This underscores the need for robust access controls and offline backups. n0n’s operations span multiple sectors, targeting organizations across 14 countries. The use of AI in crafting attacks makes traditional defenses less effective. We must evolve our security frameworks to address this shift. Stronger AI governance and zero-trust principles are critical. Teams must prioritize visibility, detection, and response to these evolving threats. The battle isn’t just about technology—it’s about strategy and resilience.

item.title: AI Agent Impersonation - Attackers Pose as ChatGPT, Claude
item.description: On Cequence: Attackers are already exploiting AI agent impersonation to steal credentials. Cequence observed a single actor posing as over 32 different AI bots, including ChatGPT and Claude, while probing for sensitive data. This activity targeted a wide range of industries and persisted for weeks. The impersonators used predictable patterns, making it clear that self-reported identities are no longer reliable. The malicious scanner rotated through multiple AI bot identities, ignoring common secret storage locations like .env files and cloud credential files. It sent bursts of requests to test which agents a business might trust, then impersonated them. Real AI bots behave predictably, but these fake agents broke almost every pattern, using shared addresses and technical fingerprints to mask their activity. Verifying AI agent identities is critical to agentic AI security. We must move beyond self-reported names and focus on behavior-based validation. Signed requests, published address ranges, and direct integrations offer better assurance. Also, watch for anomalies like agents requesting configuration files or accessing sensitive data. IP blocklists are ineffective against this dynamic threat. Agentic AI governance must ensure we know which agents are real and what they’re allowed to do. Behavior-based bot management is essential to detect and block impersonation attempts. As more businesses grant AI agents access, the need for robust verification and governance grows stronger.

item.title: Your AI Stack Is Exposed. Make It Unreachable.
item.description: On Dark Reading: Your AI stack is exposed. Make it unreachable. MCP and LLM gateways are new attack surfaces that patching alone can't secure. Zero Trust Workload Connectivity is the answer. These gateways are well connected by design. An MCP gateway can invoke tools across repositories, databases, and deployment systems. An LLM gateway may hold multiple provider keys and run with cloud permissions. Both are prime targets for unauthenticated attacks. AI is accelerating the problem. Attackers find reachable services at machine speed. A Langflow flaw was exploited within hours of disclosure. The fix is to apply Zero Trust to workloads and eliminate network reachability. With Zero Trust, every connection must be authorized by identity and logged. Teams know what their AI can access and can control it. A Langflow instance with no public listener can’t be hit by an unauthenticated RCE. A vulnerability becomes a ticket, not a catastrophe.

item.title: GitHub - cisco-ai-defense/project-quarry: Detection DSL and engine for AI agents
item.description: On GitHub: Project Quarry is a new tool in the AI security space that offers a way to detect threats in agentic AI systems. It uses a rules-based approach to analyze conversations, tool calls, and event sequences. By defining rules over messages and actions, teams can identify suspicious behavior before it becomes a problem. This is especially useful in environments where AI agents handle sensitive data or make critical decisions. The framework compiles rules into symbolic automata, which are then executed against conversation data. This allows for efficient and scalable threat detection. Rules that fail to compile are caught early, ensuring that only valid rules are used in production. It’s a solid foundation for building a defense-in-depth strategy around AI agents. For enterprises, this means more control over how AI systems operate. With Project Quarry, you can enforce policies, track behavior, and respond to anomalies in real time. It also supports integration with various models, making it adaptable to different AI workflows. This is a step forward in securing the growing landscape of agentic AI.

item.title: Beyond testmetest: Native Addon Camouflage and 42 Armed GitHub Repositories Reveal a Hidden npm Publisher
item.description: On Jfrog: The testmetest campaign demonstrates how attackers weaponize supply chain trust. They used native addons as camouflage, hiding payloads in .napi_cache files decrypted at runtime. These payloads target developer machines and CI runners, avoiding detection by staying dormant until executed in trusted environments. The attack chain extends beyond npm to GitHub, where armed repositories and fake CI workflows enable automated publishing. Attackers harvested credentials, poisoned repos, and used stolen tokens to propagate further. This shows the critical need for artifact verification and CI/CD security. We must treat every native addon with suspicion, especially those labeled as placeholders. Hidden files like .napi_cache and unexpected tmp files during install are red flags. Verify all dependencies, audit workflows, and block known malicious infrastructure.

item.title: GitHub - thomasunise/argus: Open-source agentic security operations platform:
item.description: On GitHub: Argus is a powerful example of agentic AI governance in action. Its AI agents investigate without executing, maintaining control while automating detection and response. This approach ensures that no action is taken without review, aligning with the principles of Zero Trust and NIST CSF. Autonomous response playbooks operate in shadow mode, allowing you to see what actions would be taken before they're executed. This design supports audit-ready operations and reinforces compliance with ISO 27001 and other standards. It's a practical way to balance automation with oversight. The platform also includes features like canary testing and AI-driven attack simulations, which help identify vulnerabilities before they're exploited. These tools are essential for maintaining a proactive security posture and ensuring that your defenses are always up to date.

item.title: The hidden risks of fragmented AI security
item.description: On Dark Reading: The hidden risks of fragmented AI security highlight a growing problem in how enterprises manage their AI ecosystems. As more models, agents, and tools are deployed, the attack surface expands, yet governance often lags behind. This creates blind spots that attackers can exploit. Security teams typically focus on individual components, but the real risk lies in how these pieces interact. Approved models and agents can combine in ways that evade traditional controls, leading to unexpected threats. The challenge is to monitor the entire system, not just isolated parts. Governance must evolve beyond model-specific policies. It needs to address the interactions between models, agents, and MCP servers. Relying solely on built-in guardrails is risky, as these can be bypassed. Human oversight and continuous monitoring are essential to catch threats that emerge from system-wide behavior. To stay ahead, security teams must treat AI as part of the architecture. Inventory all components, enforce human approval for critical actions, and monitor runtime behavior. The supply chain also needs scrutiny, as open tooling can introduce new risks. Collaboration between vendors and enterprises will be key to securing this new landscape.

item.title: Stronger with every update: How we’re making Chrome and the web safer in the AI Era
item.description: On Blog: Chrome’s use of AI for vulnerability detection and triage exemplifies the transformative potential of AI in enterprise security operations. By deploying large language models to find and fix hundreds of security bugs at scale, Google is setting a new standard for speed and resilience. This aligns with my focus on AI security, governance, and the need for robust frameworks to manage the risks and benefits of these technologies. The process of identifying and addressing vulnerabilities has evolved from manual, time-consuming tasks to an automated, AI-driven workflow. From triaging reports to fixing bugs and releasing patches, the integration of AI has significantly reduced the time developers spend on security issues, enabling faster remediation and better protection for users. What’s most compelling is the shift toward proactive security through dynamic patching and automated updates. These innovations reduce the patch gap and ensure that fixes reach users quickly, minimizing the window for exploitation. As we continue to refine these models, the emphasis on governance and safety remains central to our approach. The broader implications for enterprise security are clear. AI-powered tools like those used in Chrome highlight the importance of structured governance, model interoperability, and continuous improvement in security practices. For organizations, this means embracing AI not just for efficiency, but for building resilient, compliant, and future-ready security operations.

item.title: GitHub - depalmar/ai-dfir-toolkit: A vendor-neutral collection of Sigma, YARA, and Suricata rules for detecting compromise of LLM applications, MCP servers, ML supply chains, AI infrastructure, AI-powered insider threats, and RAG/vector database attacks.
item.description: On GitHub: This toolkit offers a critical resource for detecting AI and ML attacks in a vendor-neutral way. As someone deeply involved in AI governance and agentic AI threats, I see the value in rules that span multiple environments and detection platforms. The emphasis on open formats like Sigma, YARA, and Suricata aligns with my focus on interoperability and enterprise readiness. The rules cover a broad range of threats from prompt injection to model supply chain attacks. This breadth is essential for addressing the evolving landscape of AI security. The inclusion of false positive handling and severity levels reflects a practical approach to deployment, which is crucial for real-world implementation. The tool's structure supports both detection and investigation, with case studies and mappings to frameworks like ATLAS and OWASP. This makes it a valuable asset for teams looking to build a comprehensive defense strategy. The open-source nature and community contributions further strengthen its relevance and adaptability.

item.title: AI Isn't Replacing SREs. It's Deskilling Them.
item.description: On Newsletter signoz: AI isn't replacing SREs. It's deskilling them. This isn't a new phenomenon. It's a pattern that's played out in industrial automation and now resurfaces in AI-driven workflows. As AI handles routine tasks like alert triage and incident resolution, SREs are losing the muscle memory needed for complex, novel outages. The irony is that the more we automate, the more we depend on the very tools that make us less prepared for the exceptions. The stakes are high. When humans only engage with the rare, complex problems, they stop building the intuition that comes from repetition and hands-on experience. This isn't just about getting slower—it's about losing the cognitive edge that separates a good SRE from a great one. The risk isn't just deskilling; it's never-skilling. Junior engineers today may never develop the foundational skills because AI handles most of the work. We need to rethink how we integrate AI. Deliberate inefficiency—letting humans handle tasks even when AI could—keeps skills sharp. And we must design systems where humans are actively engaged, not just approving recommendations. The future of SRE isn't AI replacing humans. It's AI keeping humans sharp, ready, and in control.

item.title: Cybersecurity dominates concerns among the C-suite, small businesses and the nation
item.description: On Ibm: Cybersecurity has moved from the periphery to the core of business strategy. What was once a technical issue is now a boardroom priority. With AI-driven attacks on the rise, organizations must rethink how they defend against these evolving threats. The stakes are higher than ever, and the cost of inaction is measured in millions. The shift in focus is clear. Cyber events are now the top global business risk, according to the 2024 Allianz Risk Barometer. This signals a strategic imperative for leaders across all sectors. As AI becomes more integrated into the attacker’s toolkit, the need for advanced defenses and governance frameworks has never been more urgent. Generative AI is changing the game. Attackers are using large language models to launch more sophisticated social engineering campaigns. Gartner predicts that by 2027, 17% of cyberattacks will involve generative AI. This means organizations must invest in tools and strategies that can detect and neutralize these emerging threats. The solution lies in a balance. While AI offers powerful capabilities for threat detection and response, it also introduces new risks. Leaders must prioritize governance, zero trust, and AI security to stay ahead. Cybersecurity is no longer just about protecting data—it’s about securing the future of business.

item.title: SMS of Death
item.description: On Smsofdeath: A zero-click remote DoS vulnerability in Android's telephony framework highlights the risks of unchecked input in core systems. A malformed WAP Push SMS can crash the phone app, dropping active calls including emergency ones. The flaw stems from a lack of range check when casting a long to an int, leading to a negative array size and a crash. This is not a transient issue but a persistent denial of service that can reboot the device into a recovery loop, forcing users toward a factory reset. The implications for supply chain security are clear. Core frameworks must enforce rigorous input validation to prevent such vulnerabilities. Without it, attackers can exploit weaknesses in seemingly benign protocols. This flaw affects Android 12 through 16, with a fix released in October 2026 for 14 through 17. Older devices remain vulnerable, emphasizing the need for timely patching across ecosystems. Emergency services are at risk. A device under attack cannot reliably reach 000, violating regulatory obligations in Australia and beyond. Carriers are mandated to block non-functional devices, highlighting the real-world impact of such flaws. This is not just a technical issue—it’s a critical infrastructure risk that demands immediate attention. The fix involves adding a range check before casting, which Google implemented but without fully addressing the root cause. The updated approach suppresses the crash and deletes the malicious message, breaking the reboot loop. This underscores the importance of proactive defense in supply chain security. We must ensure all systems, especially those handling critical functions, are resilient against such threats.

item.title: A Shared ChatGPT Link Could Run Attacker Code in Your Session and Read Private Chats
item.description: On The Hacker News: A shared ChatGPT link could run attacker code in the victim's session and read private chats. The flaw was reported through OpenAI's bug bounty and fixed within eight days. The attack relied on a public link containing HTML and an interactive graph that loaded a math library. This allowed the attacker to bypass the sandbox and inject code into the main ChatGpt page. The code executed with the victim's full web access, enabling the attacker to read private conversations and perform actions on their behalf. The vulnerability stemmed from three design choices that allowed untrusted HTML to bypass security boundaries. OpenAI addressed the issue by blocking the messages the attack relied on. This highlights the risks of untrusted HTML execution in LLM interfaces. Sandboxing and input validation are critical to prevent code from running in the main application. Developers must ensure all external content is properly sanitized and that cross-frame communication is strictly controlled. For users, there's no action needed. OpenAI has fixed the issue on their end. But for teams building AI systems, this serves as a reminder to prioritize security in every layer of the stack. Input validation and sandboxing are non-negotiable.

item.title: Chinese Hackers Use AI-Powered ARTEX to Target Over 200 Organizations Worldwide
item.description: On The Hacker News: Chinese state-sponsored hackers are using an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX to conduct large-scale attacks on over 200 organizations globally. This tool enables threat actors to expand their operations at speed, allowing a small team to target a wide range of entities simultaneously. The activity is linked to a group known as Vapor Panda, which has been active since 2021. The use of ARTEX with DeepSeek and a commercial LLM highlights the growing sophistication of state-sponsored cyber operations. These tools allow attackers to automate reconnaissance, exploit vulnerabilities, and move laterally within networks. A human operator oversees the process, directing agents to execute tasks like deploying web shells and extracting credentials. The scale of these attacks is evident in the number of targets impacted, including government agencies, defense contractors, and telecom providers. CrowdStrike noted that one intrusion alone consumed 1.4 billion input tokens, underscoring the automation and efficiency enabled by AI. This approach allows attackers to shift tactics in real-time, making detection and response more challenging. As ARTEX gains traction among threat actors, its developer has closed the source code, signaling the need for stronger defenses. Organizations must prioritize AI security, LLM governance, and Zero Trust principles to counter these evolving threats. The landscape is shifting fast, and we need proactive strategies to stay ahead.

item.title: Official Claude Code Extension on Cursor Marketplace Trojanized with Persistent SSH Backdoor
item.description: On The Hacker News: The supply chain is a critical attack surface, and this incident underscores the risks of auto-updates in enterprise environments. A trojanized version of the Claude Code extension was distributed through Cursor's marketplace, masquerading as a legitimate update. It installed a persistent SSH backdoor, highlighting how trusted extensions can be weaponized. The malicious update, labeled as version 2.1.313, was injected under Anthropic's official extension ID. This bypassed normal vetting processes, allowing the attacker to deploy a loader that added an SSH key and installed persistence across Windows, Linux, and macOS. The attack leverages the trust users place in extensions to compromise systems. Auto-updating mechanisms can be a double-edged sword. While they streamline operations, they also enable rapid deployment of malicious payloads. This incident shows how critical it is to implement strict vetting for updates and to monitor for anomalies. Enterprises must ensure their systems are configured to reject untrusted or unexpected updates. The removal of the malicious version and the release of 2.1.314 are steps in the right direction, but the damage already done is a stark reminder of the importance of proactive defense. Teams must adopt a zero-trust mindset, with rigorous checks for all updates, especially those from trusted sources.

item.title: Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk) is now open weight
item.description: On Mistral AI: Mistral Large 4's release introduces powerful new tools for secure agentic AI development. The model's cybersecurity capabilities and reasoning modes offer enterprises a way to balance performance and cost while maintaining control. With three reasoning modes, teams can tailor the model to their specific needs without sacrificing efficiency. The model's ability to detect and patch vulnerabilities without unnecessary refusals is a key advantage. It aligns with the principles of Zero Trust and NIST CSF, providing a trusted foundation for secure AI operations. This makes it a strong candidate for integrating into existing security frameworks and governance processes. Mistral Large 4's open-weight nature and European training give organizations sovereignty over their AI infrastructure. Customization through Mistral Forge and deployment on internal systems empower teams to build and govern AI applications independently. This is critical for maintaining compliance with standards like HIPAA and HITRUST. For enterprises looking to adopt agentic AI, Mistral Large 4 offers a practical path forward. Its performance on coding and cybersecurity benchmarks, combined with the ability to fine-tune for specific use cases, makes it a valuable asset in building secure, compliant, and efficient AI systems.

item.title: Secure code: LLMs improve, but orgs can’t rely on AI for AppSec
item.description: On TechTarget: Generative AI coding assistants are improving at writing safe code, but the security gains remain largely an illusion of pattern recognition. Veracode’s latest research shows a rise in secure coding pass rates, but this is driven by surface-level fixes like XSS, not deeper architectural reasoning. LLMs are great at catching common bugs, but they lack the context to address complex data-flow issues or supply chain risks. Human oversight remains essential. Combining AI with traditional tools like SAST and focusing on dependency management is key to real security. The code is only as safe as the ecosystem it runs in.

item.title: Hackers could poison AI models by tampering with core infrastructure
item.description: On Cybersecurity Dive: Hackers can sabotage AI models by tampering with their underlying infrastructure like firmware and software. This isn't just a theoretical risk. Eclypsium's report shows how subtle changes in runtime can bias models toward insecure behaviors. It's a critical issue that demands attention from AI labs and businesses using these systems. The runtime state of an AI model is controlled by a complex hierarchy of software, firmware, and hardware. Each layer represents a potential entry point for attackers. The host machine is the easiest target, relying on OS, kernel, and drivers. These are vulnerable to malware like rootkits that persist below the OS level. Third-party components like firmware update services and management controllers also create risks. Compromising the management plane can allow firmware changes or direct control of devices. DPUs, used by chipmakers, are especially sensitive. They can be exploited to alter a model's operating state without changing the model file itself. Eclypsium recommends securing DPUs independently and maintaining accurate inventories of all components. Trusted AI requires visibility into every part of the infrastructure stack. We need to verify components, not just assume the model boundary starts at the container.

item.title: Anthropic-Themed Phishing Emails Bypass Top Security Tools
item.description: On Dark Reading: Even the most advanced security tools can't always catch the simplest phishing attempts. A recent campaign impersonating Anthropic used basic tactics to bypass top email gateways. Attackers sent emails pretending to offer early access to Anthropic's AI tools, targeting Google and Microsoft credentials. The emails had obvious flaws like typos and grammatical errors but still managed to slip through. The phishing flow relied on short URLs, CAPTCHAs, and fake Zoom pages to trick users. Even with these weak tactics, the campaign worked because the emails used legitimate domains and avoided triggering red flags. This highlights how identity-centric defenses are critical in today's threat landscape. Security tools can't catch everything. Phishing often succeeds because it targets human behavior, not just technical flaws. Organizations need to focus on identity protection, multi-factor authentication, and least-privilege access. These measures help prevent lateral movement and data breaches after credentials are compromised. Phishing remains a top threat, and attackers are getting better at blending in. Cybersecurity Awareness Month reminds us that training and defense-in-depth are essential. By combining strong identity controls with proactive monitoring, we can reduce the risk of these attacks succeeding.

item.title: NIK C2: The new AI-enabled command-and-control framework
item.description: On Cisco Talos: NIK C2 represents a new level of adversary tradecraft by integrating AI directly into command-and-control frameworks. This allows actors to analyze stolen data in real time, generate targeted payloads, and adapt tactics on the fly. The use of OpenAI's API within the compromised session blurs the line between data exfiltration and operational intelligence. The framework’s dual-channel C2 architecture and persistent encryption make detection and takedown significantly harder. Defenders must shift from traditional signature-based methods to continuous behavioral monitoring. The ability to leverage victim systems for AI inference introduces new risks, including unintended billing and forensic exposure. As AI becomes more embedded in adversarial tools, our defenses must evolve. We need to build systems that can detect anomalous behavior, enforce strict access controls, and maintain visibility across all endpoints.
