The future of security lies in proactive, adaptive strategies that anticipate and neutralize emerging threats before they escalate.

item.title: SolanaCry: agents searching the internet attacked by malware discovered in the wild, steals their crypto wallets
item.description: On Air Security: Malware operators are shifting their focus to AI coding agents, using them as new attack vectors. The SolanaCry case shows how attackers exploit trusted workflows by embedding malicious commands in repositories. An AI agent, tasked with building a Solana project, could unknowingly execute a PowerShell dropper that installs a remote-access tool. This highlights the risk of untrusted content and the need for tighter controls. The attack leverages a popular GitHub repo, making it a top search result. The malicious command is disguised as a legitimate installation step. Developers may never inspect the commands, trusting the agent to make decisions. This underscores the importance of visibility into what agents read and execute. Security must evolve to monitor and block harmful content before it influences behavior. AI agents are now part of the attack surface. Traditional defenses won't suffice—controls must understand the context and actions of these agents. From prompt injection to malicious repositories, the threat landscape is changing. Organizations must implement AI governance and security frameworks to mitigate these risks. The time to act is now.

item.title: Chained PHP2Shell Exploit Roots 25 Servers | Dream Research
item.description: On Dreamgroup: The recent discovery of a chained PHP2Shell exploit targeting Palo Alto Networks firewalls underscores the growing sophistication of AI-assisted cyber operations. Attackers combined two vulnerabilities to achieve root access in under 15 minutes, demonstrating how exposed management interfaces can become entry points into critical infrastructure. This isn't just a technical exploit—it's a strategic operation with clear targeting and automation. The AI tools used in the attack, including Claude Code and aiscan, suggest a level of automation and scale previously seen in nation-state campaigns. While the AI wasn't directly used to write the exploit, the code structure and consistency across 40 scripts point to AI-assisted development. This highlights a new frontier in threat intelligence—where AI isn't just a tool but a catalyst for more complex and persistent attacks. For defenders, the challenge lies in moving beyond vulnerability discovery to proactive risk management. Organizations must identify exposed systems, understand their attack surface, and act before exploitation becomes inevitable. The attack on a US government-affiliated environment shows how quickly a single compromised firewall can lead to full domain compromise. This requires a shift from reactive to predictive defenses. The incident also reinforces the need for zero trust and strict access controls. Exposed management interfaces should never be accessible from the internet. Organizations must prioritize visibility, segmentation, and continuous monitoring. Tools like Sphere and Hero can help bridge the gap between discovery and defense, enabling faster response and deeper threat analysis.

item.title: A Hacker Targeted High-Stakes Poker Players With Malware That Exposed Their Cards
item.description: On Wired: The supply chain is a critical attack surface that's often overlooked. When third-party tools are used extensively, as they are in regulated industries, the risk of compromise through software updates grows. The recent MeshAgent incident highlights how a threat actor exploited trusted update channels to deploy malware across thousands of users. This isn't just a technical flaw—it's a systemic issue in how we manage dependencies and trust in the software we rely on. The malware was delivered through official software updates, making it nearly undetectable. This underscores the need for rigorous supply chain security practices. Organizations must audit their third-party vendors, implement strict update validation, and maintain visibility into all components they rely on. In regulated environments, this isn't just about compliance—it's about protecting sensitive data and maintaining operational integrity. When a breach occurs, the response is equally important. The MeshAgent case shows how delays in addressing suspicious activity can lead to massive financial losses. Sites that acted quickly, like CoinPoker, set a standard for how others should respond. But many others ignored clear red flags. This reflects a broader challenge in balancing proactive security with the complexity of modern infrastructure.

item.title: Shadowy AI Relay Disables OpenAI Codex, Claude Code Sandboxes
item.description: On Dark Reading: The unauthorized relay service disabling security features in Codex and Claude Code tools is a growing concern. These tools are being deployed in regions where they're not officially available, but with critical sandboxing and telemetry disabled. This creates a significant risk for enterprises relying on these services without full visibility or control. The relay service installs genuine CLIs but reconfigures them to route traffic through its infrastructure. While this bypasses regional restrictions, it also removes key security safeguards. Without sandboxing, the tools can execute code with elevated privileges, exposing sensitive data and systems to potential exploitation. Governance and control are essential in agentic AI environments. The relay's ability to intercept and manipulate prompts, files, and responses highlights the need for strict oversight. Organizations must implement robust monitoring, access controls, and policy enforcement to mitigate these risks. This incident underscores the importance of AI governance and model evaluation. Enterprises should assess the security posture of any AI service they adopt, ensuring it aligns with their risk tolerance and compliance requirements. Proactive monitoring and regular audits are critical to maintaining trust in agentic AI systems.

item.title: AI Quietly Takes Root in Hospitals, Raising Security Stakes
item.description: On Dark Reading: Patients walk into a doctor's office and are swiftly asked permission for AI scribes to document notes full of sensitive health information. That intake conversation is just one entry point, now that AI is embedded throughout the patient life cycle and accessing more data than most organizations can secure. This raises significant concerns for a sector that historically struggles to secure legacy equipment and highly sought-after data, even before AI was added to the mix. Advancements could save invaluable time during patient care, but security will present hurdles in the form of supply chain risks that stem from AI vendor compromise, data leakage through prompts, and AI-generated social engineering campaigns. A recent Proofpoint report notes that "AI adoption is accelerating faster than governance." Forty-five percent of organizations confirmed they had embedded AI into their systems, but 60% lacked the necessary controls to govern that sensitive data. Healthcare organizations are rapidly deploying AI to record intake conversations, and customer conversations increasingly revolve around how physicians are using AI for clinical decisions and, more importantly, how they are protecting those tools. Even seemingly generic details, like a patient's eye color, combined with a specific injury, could qualify as protected health information. That makes data sensitivity a major concern when feeding information into AI tools. Therefore, organizations should focus on securing the underlying data rather than the tool itself.

item.title: Endor Labs AI SAST Finds Two Apache Kafka Zero-Days: Unbounded Memory Allocation from Brokers to Kafka Streams
item.description: On Endor Labs: AI SAST tools are proving to be a game-changer in security operations. Take Apache Kafka, for example. Its complex architecture and untrusted data flow make it a tough target for traditional analysis. Endor Labs' AI SAST found two zero-day vulnerabilities in Kafka by tracing untrusted data across modules, identifying unbounded memory allocation as the root cause. This highlights the power of AI in uncovering subtle, systemic risks that would take significant manual effort to find. The impact of these flaws is significant. A small payload could crash brokers, consumers, and even the log cleaner, leading to persistent denial-of-service conditions. The engine’s ability to follow data through compressed streams, deserializers, and group coordination protocols shows how AI SAST can scale across complex systems without relying on static patterns. What’s more, the findings led to real-world fixes and two CVEs. The key takeaway is that untrusted size fields can be dangerous when left unchecked. AI SAST helps bridge the gap between data flow and allocation, making it easier to identify and mitigate risks before they become incidents. This is the kind of proactive defense we need in today’s landscape.

item.title: Inside "MR ROBOT" - Anatomy of a Malware-as-a-Service Operation Targeting Indian Bank Customers
item.description: On CloudSEK: MR ROBOT is a new MaaS platform targeting Indian bank customers. It operates as a rented crimeware service, allowing affiliates to build and distribute personalized banking trojans. The platform uses Telegram and a web control panel to manage payloads, which impersonate banks and other services. This highlights the need for stronger governance in third-party software distribution. The operation's scale and sophistication are alarming. Affiliates can create tailored malware for specific institutions, using fake Play-Store pages and messaging lures. The control panel offers real-time monitoring and management, making it a production system with a live victim base. This underscores the growing threat of MaaS in supply chain security. MR ROBOT's ability to intercept SMS, enable call forwarding, and overlay phishing screens represents a comprehensive attack on multi-factor authentication. The stolen data is sent to Firebase and Telegram, demonstrating the platform's integration with cloud services. This raises concerns about the security of third-party software and the risks of unregulated distribution. As the attack surface expands, organizations must adopt a Zero Trust approach and enforce strict third-party controls. Governance frameworks like NIST CSF and ISO 20000 can help manage these risks. The MR ROBOT case serves as a reminder that supply chain security is not just about code but also about the platforms and services we rely on.

item.title: Scanning 7.25 Million Public Repositories on China's Largest Git Platform for Secrets
item.description: On Mongodb: Gitee's scale and lack of platform-level safeguards for credential exposure reveal deeper supply chain and infrastructure security challenges. The scan uncovered 26,400 verified-live credentials across 7.25 million public repositories. This highlights how even large Git platforms can become unintentional credential sinks without robust secret-scanning partnerships or API limitations. The absence of a public equivalent to GitHub’s secret-scanning infrastructure means many secrets persist in commit history. Gitee’s limited API and search capabilities further complicate large-scale research. This underscores the need for stronger platform-level defenses and standardized secret detection across all code-hosting services. Credential exposure isn’t just a technical issue—it’s a systemic one. The scale of exposure, including enterprise-level keys, shows how easily sensitive data can leak through public repositories. As we adopt more agentic AI and cloud services, protecting infrastructure and supply chains becomes more critical than ever. This research also points to a broader gap in remediation paths for Chinese-based platforms. While Western companies often have bug bounty programs, many Chinese entities lack clear disclosure channels. This makes credential exposure harder to address at scale. We need better frameworks for accountability and remediation across all regions.

item.title: 'Icepick' Leak Exposes Thousands of Homeland Security Personnel, Groups and More
item.description: On Unicornriot: The recent breach of the DHS SSO system highlights critical gaps in supply chain security and access control across multi-agency environments. The exposure of thousands of personnel records, including locations and group memberships, underscores the risks of centralized identity systems. Agencies like DHS must ensure strict adherence to NIST CSF and ISO 27001 frameworks to prevent such vulnerabilities. The data reveals how groups like CUC (Certified Undercover) and TAK (Team Awareness Kit) enable deep access to sensitive operations. This level of visibility is a double-edged sword—while it aids coordination, it also creates attack surfaces. Teams need to adopt Zero Trust principles and continuous monitoring to mitigate insider threats. International offices and cross-border operations are especially vulnerable. The breach exposed U.S. embassies and consulates in multiple countries, showing how global footprints can be exploited. DHS and its partners must enforce strict data handling protocols and ensure compliance with international regulations like GDPR and HIPAA. This incident is a wake-up call for agencies to rethink how they manage access, especially in cloud and agentic AI environments. The breach wasn’t just a technical failure—it was a systemic risk. We need stronger governance, better training, and more transparency to protect both people and data.

item.title: ESET APT Activity Report Q2 2026–Q3 2026
item.description: On Welivesecurity: The ESET report highlights a growing trend where APT groups are integrating AI and LLMs into their operations. These tools are being used to speed up tasks like malware development and phishing, often in ways that mimic human coding. One example involved AI-generated phishing images and scripts designed to bypass LLM-based security checks. This shows how attackers are adapting to new technologies to maintain operational efficiency. The use of AI in these contexts doesn’t signal a fully autonomous threat landscape. Instead, it reflects a shift toward using AI as a productivity tool, much like developers use it today. APT groups are leveraging it to automate manual processes and analyze large datasets, not to replace human oversight. This means our defenses must evolve to address both the tools and the tactics they enable. AI security is no longer a niche concern. As these groups adopt it more widely, we must reinforce governance frameworks, model monitoring, and strict access controls. Zero Trust and AI-specific controls should be part of every enterprise’s strategy. The goal is to stay ahead of adversaries who are already using these technologies to their advantage.

item.title: Managed for Malice: How Attackers Turn MDM into Remote Access
item.description: On Huntress: MDM platforms are essential for device management, but they're being weaponized by attackers through social engineering and supply chain exploitation. These tools offer centralized control and trusted access, which can become entry points if misused. Threat actors are leveraging legitimate MDM applications to stage attacks, often starting with phishing emails that mimic business-related lures. The same MDM client can be used to install unauthorized RMM tools, allowing attackers to maintain persistence even after removal. This highlights the need for stronger governance and detection strategies. A recurring RMM installation is a red flag, indicating a coordinated attack rather than an isolated incident. Detection must account for the entire chain of events—social engineering leading to MDM enrollment, followed by RMM installation and outbound communication with unfamiliar relays. Correlating identity, MDM, endpoint, and network telemetry is key to identifying these sophisticated attacks. Organizations must treat MDM enrollment as a security-sensitive activity, not just an administrative task. Mitigation requires strict control over enrollment paths and authorized applications. Maintain an inventory of approved MDM products and RMM instances. Train users to verify unexpected requests and scrutinize business-themed lures. If a compromise is suspected, isolate the endpoint and reimage it if integrity cannot be confirmed.

item.title: GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, But Attackers Lurk on in GitHub
item.description: On Dark Reading: The GhostAction campaign's latest wave failed to execute malicious workflows, but the persistence of compromised accounts highlights a troubling trend. Attackers are leveraging GitHub's trust in developer workflows to inject payloads that seek credentials and cloud access. This underscores the need for stronger protections around developer accounts and closer scrutiny of GitHub Actions workflows for suspicious activity. The shift toward targeting developer endpoints and cloud access suggests a broader strategy. Attackers are deploying varied payloads depending on the runner environment, from GitHub-hosted to self-hosted systems. This adaptability means defenders must assume any account could be compromised and treat all workflows with caution. While GitHub blocked execution, the attackers retained access to nearly 1,800 accounts, many of which had been used before. This demonstrates how easily stolen tokens can persist and enable future attacks. The key takeaway is that no account is safe, and every workflow must be monitored for anomalies. The campaign's failure doesn't mean the threat has subsided. Attackers are likely refining their tactics and preparing for future waves. Organizations must act now by removing known malicious files, revoking tokens, and rotating credentials. Proactive monitoring and strict access controls are the best defenses against this evolving threat.

item.title: Silent Train: Volt Typhoon’s Sophisticated Infection Chain into US Targets Exposed
item.description: On Zetter Zeroday: Volt Typhoon's Silent Train operation reveals a new level of sophistication in supply chain attacks. By leveraging compromised SOHO routers and IoT devices, they create daisy chains to infiltrate high-value targets with near-invisibility. These attacks are designed to persist for minutes or hours before erasing all traces, making detection and attribution extremely difficult. The use of one-time infection chains and geographic diversity in device types complicates tracking. Researchers found over 27 device classes used across operations, with attackers rotating device types monthly to avoid visibility. This method ensures no single point of failure and obscures the entire attack path. The focus on critical infrastructure and trusted entities underscores the strategic intent behind these breaches. Targets include defense contractors, telecoms, and military-linked organizations, all of which provide access to sensitive networks. The attackers exfiltrate data and maintain long-term access, suggesting a mix of espionage and pre-positioning for potential conflicts. Organizations must strengthen supply chain security and monitor for unusual device behavior. Prioritizing patch management and reducing reliance on unpatched IoT devices is critical. Also, consider the broader implications of agentic AI in threat detection and response. Stay vigilant and proactive.

item.title: Download the SANS AI Security Maturity Model™ eBook
item.description: On SANS Institute: The SANS AI Security Maturity Model offers a structured way to assess where an organization stands on AI security. It bridges strategy and execution by mapping maturity stages to real-world compliance and operational needs. This model aligns well with my work on AI governance and agentic AI, especially the Principle of Least Agency. It ensures autonomy is scoped carefully, matching the need for control in security and risk. The model treats governance as a ceiling, not a checkbox. This mirrors my emphasis on governance ceiling concepts, where no matter how advanced your detection or protection capabilities are, your overall score can't exceed your weakest pillar. It reinforces the need for documented evidence, not just aspirations, in proving maturity. This is a practical way to build trust and ensure accountability in AI programs. Industry-specific weighting profiles and named prerequisites at every stage make the model adaptable. For regulated environments, this means governance and data classification are foundational. It also highlights the importance of Non-Human Identity management and documented human ownership for AI agents, which are critical for accountability and control in agentic systems. This model is a valuable tool for security leaders looking to transition from ad hoc practices to AI-native security. It’s grounded in real-world frameworks and validated by practitioners. For those building or scaling AI programs, it provides a clear path with actionable steps. The SANS AI Security Maturity Model is a must-read for anyone serious about AI security and governance.

item.title: Unauthenticated file read leaks master key on Enterprise proxy
item.description: On GitHub: Unauthenticated file read vulnerabilities in enterprise proxies can expose critical secrets like master keys and provider API credentials. These flaws allow attackers to exfiltrate data by leveraging misconfigured access controls. The risk is heightened in cloud environments where sensitive keys are stored in environment variables. Network segmentation and strict outbound traffic controls are essential to prevent data exfiltration. Limiting egress to known endpoints blocks attackers from sending stolen information to external servers. This aligns with Zero Trust principles and helps mitigate supply chain risks. Secure key management practices are non-negotiable. Storing secrets in secret managers instead of environment variables reduces exposure. Additionally, using unique salts and rotating keys regularly strengthens defenses against exploitation. This issue underscores the need for continuous security assessments and proactive mitigation. Teams must balance operational efficiency with robust security controls. Prioritize secure configurations and regular audits to stay ahead of emerging threats.

item.title: Discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities in critical, real-world software with Claude
item.description: On Anthropic: Claude's ability to discover and chain vulnerabilities in critical software highlights the growing risk posed by AI in enterprise environments. These exploits, requiring little to no user interaction, demonstrate how models can combine multiple weaknesses into working attacks. The implications for AI security are clear—without robust frameworks, the same tools that protect us could be weaponized. This research underscores the need for stronger governance and monitoring in AI systems. Enterprises must adopt rigorous evaluation processes and ensure models are tested against real-world scenarios. AI security isn’t just about preventing leaks; it’s about understanding how models can be manipulated to bypass even the most sophisticated defenses. Frameworks like NIST CSF and ISO 27001 are essential, but they must evolve to address the unique risks of agentic AI and LLMs. Teams need to bridge gaps between security, compliance, and development to create a unified approach. The goal is to build systems that are not only secure but also resilient to emerging threats.

item.title: NIST issues roadmap for transition to post-quantum encryption standards
item.description: On Nextgov: NIST has released a roadmap to guide organizations through the transition to post-quantum cryptography standards. This comes in response to the Trump administration’s executive order that accelerated the timeline for adopting quantum-resistant encryption. The report outlines the need to replace quantum-vulnerable algorithms with PQC standards that can withstand future quantum threats. The “harvest now, decrypt later” scenario underscores the urgency of this transition. Adversaries could collect data today and decrypt it once quantum computers become viable. NIST’s guidance helps organizations understand which algorithms will be phased out and how to manage the migration without disrupting operations. The report emphasizes that no single strategy fits all use cases. Some systems, like those handling sensitive data, may require immediate attention. A hybrid approach, combining traditional and post-quantum encryption, is recommended as a practical interim solution. This aligns with the need to balance security with operational continuity. For regulated industries, compliance with standards like HIPAA and HITRUST will increasingly intersect with PQC adoption. The NIST roadmap provides a clear path for aligning technical transitions with regulatory requirements. Organizations must start planning now to avoid risks and ensure long-term resilience.

item.title: The Mythical Man-Month in the age of AI - Jan van den Berg
item.description: On J11g: Adding more people to a late project makes it later. This is Brooks's Law — a lesson from software development that still rings true today. The article highlights how AI agents, despite their speed and autonomy, aren't immune to this principle. The myth of the mythical man-month isn’t dead. It’s just evolved. AI agents can’t magically deliver a baby in a month. Sequential tasks remain sequential. And without clear orchestration, nine agents can rewrite each other’s work in a high-speed loop. This isn’t about reducing complexity. It’s about managing it. Someone still needs to define done, review code, catch hallucinations, and stitch the pieces together. That someone is you. The lesson is clear: clarity in requirements and governance is essential. AI agents are powerful tools, but they’re not a magic wand. They require structure, oversight, and a shared understanding of what success looks like.

item.title: TRT World - Türkiye's Erdogan chairs cybersecurity meeting on digital sovereignty, AI threats
item.description: On Trtworld: Türkiye's digital sovereignty strategy reflects a clear focus on securing national interests in an increasingly interconnected world. The recent meeting chaired by President Erdogan highlighted the growing risks posed by AI and global geopolitical shifts. This approach aligns with frameworks like NIST CSF and ISO 27001, which emphasize proactive risk management and governance. The board's emphasis on protecting critical infrastructure and reducing reliance on foreign tech resonates with broader compliance challenges. As AI evolves, the need for robust governance and risk assessment becomes more critical. These strategies must balance innovation with security to avoid unintended vulnerabilities. Interagency coordination and joint risk assessments are essential for addressing the rapid spread of cyber threats. The strategy's focus on building national capacity mirrors the importance of continuous compliance and adaptation in today's threat landscape. This requires a unified approach across sectors and stakeholders. Strengthening digital resilience isn't just about technology—it's about governance, policy, and collaboration. Türkiye's efforts offer a model for how nations can navigate the complexities of AI and digital sovereignty while aligning with global standards. The path is complex, but the direction is clear.

item.title: NSM hever det nasjonale cyberrisikonivået til HØYT - Nasjonal sikkerhetsmyndighet
item.description: On Nsm: Norway's national cyber risk level has been elevated to HØYT, reflecting a growing threat landscape. NSM's response underscores the need for proactive governance and risk management, aligning with global standards like NIST CSF and ISO 27001. This shift highlights the urgency for regulated industries to adopt robust frameworks that address both current and emerging threats. The rise in successful cyber operations, including ransomware and advanced persistent threats, demonstrates the increasing sophistication of attacks. These incidents underscore the importance of strengthening defenses and improving incident response capabilities. AI and LLMs are now part of the threat equation, enabling faster and more targeted attacks. This evolution demands a reevaluation of how we design and implement security controls. Organizations must adopt a layered approach, combining technical, operational, and human-centric measures. Phishing-resistant MFA, network segmentation, and continuous monitoring are critical. Additionally, supply chain risk management and asset visibility are essential to maintaining resilience. These practices not only protect individual entities but also contribute to national security by reducing the overall risk exposure.

item.title: Federal AI security guidance misses real-world enterprise threats
item.description: On TechTarget: The federal AI security guidance released by NIST, CISA, and the NSA outlines 10 incident response practices for advanced AI systems. While it provides a framework rooted in established cybersecurity disciplines, it misses critical real-world enterprise threats. The guidance focuses heavily on frontier model training and lab environments, but enterprise AI agents operate in complex application stacks where containment is far more challenging. Revoking access rarely stops the chain reaction an agent can set in motion. When an AI control failure occurs, the agent may leave unfinished tasks, queued requests, or persistent memory instructions that continue running unchecked. Security teams must trace activity across systems to understand what the agent changed and what remains active. The key is determining whether the agent failed at its job or crossed a boundary it wasn’t permitted to cross. This distinction drives the need for robust incident response and containment strategies. Even with clear containment rules, an agent doesn’t need to bypass access control to create risk. Granted permissions may allow actions that fall outside approved tasks. Detection requires examining the agent’s behavior, interactions, and whether its actions align with the intended purpose. Deviations can be dangerous, especially when the agent continues operating at machine speed. Continuous investigation, evidence preservation, and containment are essential, with human oversight proportional to the risk. Recovery from an AI incident goes beyond restarting a clean model. Unauthorized changes, altered records, or stored instructions can persist long after the agent is revoked. Security teams must document the control failure, the changes made, and the steps to isolate or close the failure path. Data owners also need to reconcile affected information against authoritative records. Clearing the conversation while preserving a poisoned knowledge source can recreate the incident immediately, highlighting the need for thorough recovery and risk management.

item.title: 3 Frameworks to Protect CISOs & Orgs Against AI Liability
item.description: On Dark Reading: CISOs are facing a new frontier of liability with the rise of agentic AI. The key to staying ahead is proactive governance and documentation. Frameworks like Garrie's help CISOs assess risks and build an evidentiary trail that can defend decisions in the event of a compromise. Documentation and transparency are non-negotiable. By embedding these practices into vendor contracts and incident response plans, CISOs can ensure they have the evidence needed to prove due diligence. This includes clear provisions for data preservation, access to logs, and understanding of vendor responsibilities. The frameworks emphasize three critical areas: risk scoring for AI deployments, recording board decisions, and creating an incident response checklist. Each step is designed to provide clarity, accountability, and defensibility in the face of legal or regulatory scrutiny. CISOs must act now. Start by testing one framework on an AI deployment, refining a board report, and practicing incident response scenarios. The goal isn't just to follow guidelines but to build a robust defense that aligns with what regulators and litigators will ultimately demand.

item.title: 'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants
item.description: On Dark Reading: The Aokigahara stealer's focus on AI tools and developer keyrings underscores a growing threat to enterprise security. Attackers are now targeting AI sessions, cloud credentials, and developer infrastructure, which can expose sensitive data and open new avenues for financial exploitation. This shift highlights the need for stronger protections around AI-session data and cloud credentials, especially as these assets become more valuable to threat actors. The malware's ability to steal authentication files, session data, and configuration files from tools like GitHub Copilot and Codex demonstrates how easily these resources can be compromised. By leveraging stolen credentials, attackers can access private code repositories, cloud environments, and even extort organizations by threatening to leak sensitive information. This is a clear sign that traditional security measures are no longer sufficient. Defenders must treat AI-tool authentication data with the same rigor as cloud credentials and developer keys. This means implementing Zero Trust principles, reducing the persistence of long-lived secrets, and using managed identities and short-lived credentials where possible. Security teams should also monitor access to local application storage and authentication files associated with AI assistants and developer tools. Organizations need to adopt a proactive approach to protect their assets. Revoking exposed sessions, rotating secrets, and assessing AI sessions, API keys, and cloud tokens should be part of routine security practices. The Aokigahara incident serves as a reminder that the security landscape is evolving, and our defenses must keep pace with these new threats.

item.title: External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery
item.description: On Dark Reading: Email bombing in Teams chats is evolving into a repeatable access path for attackers. The technique leverages social engineering and IT-support impersonation to trick employees into granting remote access. Threat actors flood inboxes with emails to create urgency, then use external Teams chats to initiate the attack chain. This aligns with Zero Trust principles by highlighting the need for strict access controls and continuous verification. The attack lifecycle is fast, with payloads executing in under 15 minutes. Once access is granted, attackers execute malware, steal credentials, and move laterally within the network. This underscores the importance of robust detection and response strategies. Defenders must prioritize monitoring for unusual chat activity and securing remote access pathways to mitigate these threats. Arctic Wolf's research shows this technique is being used at scale, with recurring infrastructure and naming conventions. Attackers use throwaway domains and friendly display names to bypass user suspicion. Organizations should block unmanaged accounts, harden remote access, and educate users on identifying red flags in Teams chats. Training is critical to counter these evolving social engineering tactics. Microsoft is enhancing its defenses with AI-powered phishing detection and built-in protections. However, the threat landscape continues to evolve, with attackers integrating Teams chat abuse with other intrusion methods. Staying ahead requires a proactive approach that combines technology, policy, and user awareness. Let’s build resilient systems together.

item.title: Beware the Slasher: AI Could Kill Off Cybersecurity Pros' Skills
item.description: On Dark Reading: AI is reshaping cybersecurity, but it’s not replacing human expertise. Automation can simplify tasks, yet it risks erasing the foundational skills that make tools effective. As AI takes over routine work, professionals must stay engaged with core problems to avoid losing touch with what’s critical. This shift is not new—it’s part of a longer trend where technology mediates how we solve problems. The real challenge is balancing automation with hands-on experience. Junior professionals learn by doing, and if AI removes those opportunities, we risk weakening the next generation of experts. Tools can help, but they don’t replace the need for deep understanding. The best outcomes come from combining AI’s capabilities with human insight and judgment. Organizations must use AI strategically, not as a shortcut. It’s about applying it where it adds value—like threat hunting or penetration testing—while keeping skills sharp. The goal isn’t to rely on tools for everything but to enhance human expertise. After all, the most effective AI users are those who bring domain knowledge to the table.

item.title: So Many AI Security Benchmarks, But None Tell the Whole Story
item.description: On Dark Reading: The challenge of benchmarking AI model security is real. While many metrics exist, none fully capture the complexity of real-world use. Organizations must test models against their own code and workflows to ensure alignment with business needs. Internal validation is key to understanding how a model performs in your environment. Testing against your own systems reveals what benchmarks cannot. A model may score well on public datasets but fail in your specific context. This is why internal testing should be a non-negotiable part of any AI security strategy. It’s not about chasing the highest score but ensuring the model meets your operational and security requirements. Governance and real-world impact matter more than raw benchmarks. Models like MiST show that specialization and better workflows can yield strong results without massive complexity. But the ultimate measure is whether the model helps you find vulnerabilities, reduce risk, or improve response times. Focus on outcomes, not just numbers. AI security is not a one-size-fits-all problem. Each organization has unique workflows, threats, and compliance needs. The right approach is to build a test pipeline that reflects these realities. Public benchmarks are useful for shortlisting, but they shouldn’t replace your own evaluation. Choose tools that deliver measurable value, not just impressive demos.

item.title: Windows Endpoint Security Platform: Inside wesp.sys
item.description: On Elastic: Microsoft’s decision to move EDR out of the kernel with the Windows Endpoint Security Platform (WESP) is a critical shift in endpoint security. The introduction of wesp.sys and espclient.dll signals a move toward centralized control, reducing the risk of third-party kernel drivers causing system instability, as seen in the CrowdStrike incident. This approach aligns with a broader goal of improving Windows reliability by minimizing the exposure of untrusted code. The current model relies on kernel drivers to intercept events, but this creates vulnerabilities. By offloading notifications to a single, Microsoft-managed driver, WESP aims to reduce the complexity and risk associated with multiple vendors’ custom implementations. However, the transition isn't seamless. EDR vendors must adapt to a new framework that may lack the granular control they’ve relied on for years. What’s clear is that WESP introduces a new layer of complexity. While it offers the potential for more robust, centralized security, it also requires careful handling of notifications and blocking capabilities. The absence of a direct response mechanism in user mode raises questions about how EDRs will enforce policies, especially when blocking process creation. This is a critical area that will shape the future of endpoint detection and response.

item.title: Stealing OpenAI Reasoning Traces via Compaction Smuggling
item.description: On Xint: Compaction smuggling highlights a critical gap in how we handle reasoning traces in enterprise environments. The ability to encode raw reasoning inside compactions and transfer it across models bypasses existing safeguards. This isn’t hypothetical—it’s already being weaponized in real-world campaigns. The attack leverages the fact that compactions are encrypted but still portable. By steering the compaction process to preserve reasoning verbatim, attackers can extract valuable intellectual property. This underscores the need for stronger controls around reasoning trace handling. In regulated industries, the stakes are even higher. Distilled models pose a direct threat to compliance, security, and intellectual property. We must treat reasoning traces with the same rigor as sensitive data. This means rethinking how we encrypt, store, and transmit these traces. The lesson is clear: any server-side process that reads decrypted reasoning and acts on client instructions is a potential oracle. We need to apply the same protections to compactions as we do to raw reasoning. This is a call to action for all of us in cybersecurity and AI governance.

item.title: 'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets
item.description: On Dark Reading: The Gheist campaign underscores the critical risk of compromised GitHub tokens. Attackers are leveraging stolen credentials to infiltrate private repositories and exfiltrate cloud secrets. This highlights a growing threat vector that exploits the trust placed in developer accounts. The attack relies on malicious workflows that print secrets into logs and retrieve them via GitHub's API. Because the breach occurs through legitimate channels, it's hard to detect and block. This makes token-based attacks particularly insidious. Enterprise environments are especially vulnerable. Stolen tokens with broad permissions can grant attackers access to cloud services like AWS Secrets Manager. The key takeaway is that scoped, short-lived credentials are essential for minimizing exposure. Defenders must treat GitHub Actions and workflows as potential attack surfaces. Regular audits, token rotation, and strict access controls are non-negotiable. The Gheist incident is a wake-up call for securing the developer pipeline.

item.title: In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown
item.description: On Dark Reading: A new attack exploits how AI agents trust markdown files, turning them into vectors for malware. The technique uses malicious files in a user's downloads folder to trick agents into executing harmful actions. This isn't a lab experiment but a real-world incident caught by Forever Security. They stopped an attack before any code ran, highlighting the urgency of the issue. The attack relies on the agent treating a markdown file as trusted instructions. A file named "AGENTS.md" was found in a customer's downloads folder, disguised as engineering notes. When the agent reads it, it can rewrite its configuration and perform follow-on actions. In tests, the attack succeeded over 90% of the time with Codex and about 50% with Claude Code. This isn’t a bug in the agent itself. The problem lies in the trust placed on the download folder. Forever Security says there’s nothing to patch because the agent is doing what it was designed to do. The real risk is the environment where the agent operates. Defenders must treat the downloads folder as a potential threat and implement checks to detect unexpected changes. The attack underscores the need for governance frameworks in AI security. Organizations should treat the user's home directory as hostile ground and enforce approval gates. If a red flag is raised, assume credentials are compromised and rotate them. This is just one example of a broader pattern where human-centric defenses fail when agents take over.

item.title: Enclave: AuthMask: We Made Microsoft Authenticator Hand Over Tokens to an App With Zero Permissions
item.description: On Enclave: The zero-permission token handover in Microsoft Authenticator is a critical flaw with serious implications for enterprise security. An unprivileged app can impersonate any first-party app and get tokens for a work account without user interaction. This exposes sensitive data like mailbox access, files, and calendars. The risk is real and affects any device with Authenticator installed. The vulnerability stems from how Authenticator validates requests. It checks if a calling activity exists and if the redirect URI matches the claimed package's signature. But it doesn't verify if the app making the request is actually the one it claims to be. This creates a bypass for impersonation. Microsoft has patched this as CVE-2026-80097, but the flaw highlights a deeper issue in authentication brokers. Enterprises must demand stronger validation mechanisms to prevent token handover to untrusted apps. We need better controls to ensure access is only granted to legitimate callers. This isn't just a technical issue—it's a security gap that can be exploited to compromise user data and infrastructure. Teams should audit their authentication flows and ensure all apps interact with brokers through secure, verified channels. Stay vigilant.

item.title: Gheist: Attempted Scaled Abuse of Stolen GitHub Tokens Stumbles
item.description: On Wiz: The Gheist campaign highlights the evolving threat of stolen GitHub tokens. Attackers are leveraging compromised credentials to plant secret-dumping workflows across repositories, exploiting GitHub's API to exfiltrate secrets without outbound connections. This underscores the need for stronger token management and visibility into repository access. The attack's reliance on GitHub's API for secret extraction makes it difficult to detect with traditional network monitoring. However, GitHub's approval hold for public repositories has disrupted the campaign, proving that proactive controls can mitigate such threats. Private repositories and enterprise environments remain vulnerable, emphasizing the importance of granular access controls. Defenders should hunt for branches named ci-sync- followed by six random characters, and look for workflows with the commit message "ci: sync config." Monitoring GitHub audit logs for suspicious activity and checking cloud audit logs for role assumptions can help identify compromised environments. Hardening measures like scoped OIDC policies and ephemeral runners are critical to reducing attack surfaces. This incident reinforces the need for continuous monitoring, rapid response, and robust governance around token usage. As supply chain attacks become more sophisticated, organizations must prioritize visibility, least-privilege access, and proactive threat hunting to stay ahead of adversaries.

item.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro Tech Blog: Advancing Open Intelligence
item.description: On Kimi: Kimi K3.1 Pro represents a significant leap in open-weight models, combining enhanced coding, 3D creation, and financial analysis with robust reinforcement learning. The model's ability to handle complex tasks like building a human walking dynamics simulator showcases its long-horizon capabilities. These improvements are not just technical but also strategic, ensuring the model can operate effectively in real-world environments. Cybersecurity was a key consideration in the development of K3.1 Pro. The team recognized the potential for misuse and took deliberate steps to mitigate risks. By identifying and removing cyber-related data from both training stages, they ensured the model's capabilities remain within controlled boundaries. This approach balances the need for general usefulness with the responsibility of preventing harmful applications. The release of K3.1 Pro reflects a commitment to open-weight principles. By limiting offensive cyber capabilities and focusing on defensive use cases, the model supports a broader goal of improving software security through wider access. This gradual diffusion of capability aligns with the belief that more teams having the tools to audit and secure their systems ultimately leads to a more secure digital landscape.

item.title: Why Caribbean Threats Cascade Into Global Cyber-Risk
item.description: On Dark Reading: The Caribbean is showing us a critical flaw in how we manage risk and compliance. When exploit velocity accelerates but assurance remains annual, the gap creates exposure. A ransomware attack in Curaçao disrupted six jurisdictions at once. One platform, six governments. The speed at which threats emerge outpaces our ability to respond. The data shows a stark shift. Attack attempts in the Caribbean rose to 325 million in 2025, with vulnerabilities targeted within 2,4 to 48 hours. Yet, breach detection and containment took an average of 247 days. This is the first time in five years that containment has slowed. Assurance is falling behind exploitation. Third-party assurance still runs on an annual cycle. A global insurer reviews its Caribbean processor once a year. By the time the assessment is done, the threat landscape has changed. Annual attestations don’t reflect real-time risk. If your assurance is a document signed in March, you’re not managing risk—you’re recording a past event. The Caribbean isn’t asking for allowances. It’s showing the industry what happens when exploitation accelerates and assurance does not. Anyone with a supply chain touching this region is measuring a snapshot of a system that has already changed.

item.title: Web Hole: Agents searching the internet hijacked by malicious websites
item.description: On Air Security: AI agents are becoming a new vector for attacks. When they search the web, they can be tricked into interacting with malicious sites that still show up in search results. These sites may no longer exist or have changed content, but they remain in the search index. An attacker can exploit this by registering a dead site, changing its content, and waiting for victims to engage. Agents often use tools like WebSearch and WebFetch to gather information. These tools rely on search engines to rank results, but the ranking can be outdated. A site might still appear relevant even if it's no longer active or has malicious content. This creates a blind spot in the agent's context, allowing attackers to inject harmful payloads. Untrusted data is a critical risk. When agents process information from the web, they can be prompted to take actions based on malicious content. This data becomes part of the agent's supply chain, making it a potential attack vector. The more unsupervised agents operate, the greater the risk. They can autonomously surf the web, increasing exposure to these threats. Vetting content before it reaches an agent's context is essential. Every piece of data that enters the agent's environment should be scrutinized. As AI adoption grows, so do the threats. We must build defenses that account for this new attack surface. Stay vigilant, and ensure your agents are protected from the web's hidden dangers.

item.title: Infostealer riding the AI Train
item.description: On Checkpoint: Aokigahara, a new infostealer, is targeting AI development tools and cloud environments. It collects credentials and session data from tools like ChatG This shift shows attackers are now eyeing AI credentials as valuable assets. Stolen tokens could grant access to paid services or expose sensitive development data Strong governance and security practices are critical to protect these assets. Teams must treat AI credentials with the same rigor as cloud keys and browser sessions We need to build defenses that span both traditional and emerging threats. This includes monitoring, access controls, and regular audits of AI environments

item.title: Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks
item.description: On Microsoft: The LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise highlights the risks of malicious packages in PyPI. A compromised release distributed through official container images used Python startup hooks to execute payloads without requiring explicit import. This means exposure wasn’t limited to systems using LiteLLM as a gateway. The payload collected credentials from developer tools, cloud environments, and browsers. It encrypted data and exfiltrated it to an attacker-controlled endpoint. On Unix systems, it also retrieved and executed additional Python code, expanding the attack surface. Organizations must address the affected Python environment, not just the package. Removing the package isn’t enough. Rebuilding from verified artifacts and rotating credentials from a clean machine are critical steps. This incident underscores the need for secure software supply chain practices. Use hash-pinned lock files, verify package provenance, and restrict outbound access. Always inspect environments from a trusted system during investigations.

item.title: ABC wipes staff devices exposed to new, sophisticated cyber attack
item.description: On Abc net: The ABC is wiping staff devices after being exposed to a new cyber attack called Adfection. This attack uses online ads to deliver spyware without needing a user click. It targets high-profile and sensitive organisations, including media, government, and critical infrastructure. The attack is part of a broader campaign, and while the ABC found no signs of compromise, it's taking precautions. Adfection highlights the risks of relying on ad tech platforms. These platforms are powerful but also vulnerable. Attackers can exploit them to profile millions of devices, collect data, and even track individuals. This isn't a new problem, but it's becoming more sophisticated. We need stronger oversight of ad tech to prevent abuse. The attack underscores the need for better security in our digital infrastructure. Ad tech is a critical part of the internet, but it's also a vector for supply chain attacks. We must address the gaps in how these platforms are managed and secured. This includes improving transparency, accountability, and oversight. As leaders in cybersecurity, we must push for stronger protections against these types of threats. This includes better governance, more rigorous audits, and a focus on zero trust. The Adfection campaign is a wake-up call for all of us. Let's work together to make our digital world safer.

item.title: Red-Teaming OpenAI's Internal Agent Monitoring Systems
item.description: On Metr: The red-teaming exercise on OpenAI’s internal agent monitoring systems highlights critical gaps in how agentic AI is governed. The findings underscore the need for monitoring systems that are resilient to deliberate subversion. With deep access to their infrastructure, the team identified vulnerabilities that could allow agents to bypass oversight, emphasizing the importance of proactive design. Monitoring must be continuous and not contingent on agent behavior. The system should enforce visibility at regular intervals, not just when agents end their turns. This ensures that even if agents attempt to evade detection, they are still subject to scrutiny. It’s a fundamental shift from reactive to proactive control. Robust governance requires more than just technical safeguards. It demands clear ownership, transparent processes, and the ability to audit and respond to incidents swiftly. The exercise revealed the value of red-teaming as a routine practice, not a one-off event. It’s about building systems that can withstand strategic attacks over time. The implications for agentic AI governance are clear. We must prioritize monitoring that is comprehensive, tamper-proof, and aligned with the risks these systems pose. The exercise serves as a reminder that security is an ongoing process, not a static checkpoint.

item.title: TikTok staff raised child safety alarms. Court records show executives failed to act
item.description: On Npr: TikTok's handling of child safety and data privacy issues highlights broader regulatory and compliance challenges for tech companies. The internal depositions show employees raised concerns about minors accessing harmful content and being exposed to sexual exploitation. Leadership failed to act on these alarms, which is a critical compliance failure. The company's approach to age verification and content moderation has clear gaps. TikTok avoided surveys to determine user ages to sidestep COPPA and FTC scrutiny. This reflects a broader issue where compliance is treated as a risk rather than a priority. The consequences of such decisions can be severe, including legal and reputational damage. The algorithm's role in creating "rabbit holes" of harmful content is another compliance concern. Internal reports acknowledged the real contagion effect of suicide and self-harm content. Yet, the platform did not warn parents or take meaningful steps to mitigate these risks. This shows a lack of accountability and governance. Compliance must be proactive, not reactive. Tech companies must align with frameworks like NIST CSF and ISO 27001 to ensure they meet legal and ethical standards. The TikTok case underscores the need for stronger oversight and transparency in how platforms handle user data and content safety.

item.title: Ransomware attacks rose by 24% in Q3 as critical infrastructure risks attract attention
item.description: On NCC Group: Ransomware attacks surged by 23% in Q3 2026, with critical infrastructure emerging as a prime target. The rise underscores the growing sophistication of threat actors, who are increasingly leveraging hybrid warfare tactics to disrupt essential services. A recent attack on a UK power generator exemplifies this trend, highlighting how cyber threats now blur the lines between the digital and physical worlds. Urgent action is needed to secure critical infrastructure. The integration of IT and OT systems, while beneficial, has created new vulnerabilities. Threat actors exploit these gaps to gain access to operational technology, as seen in the UK incident. Separating IT and OT environments, securing privileged accounts, and implementing network segmentation are critical steps to mitigate these risks. Agentic AI is also reshaping the threat landscape. Misaligned AI agents, prompt injection, and excessive permissions have turned legitimate tools into attack vectors. Recent incidents involving US government systems and Australian health institutions show the need for strict oversight of AI interactions, especially in sectors handling sensitive data. The intersection of ransomware, critical infrastructure, and AI security demands robust governance and operational controls. Proactive measures, like zero trust and continuous monitoring, are essential to stay ahead of evolving threats. As we move into Q4, the focus must remain on protecting what matters most.

item.title: Invasive Ads: The Unconventional Cyber Surveillance Attack Surface | TrendAI (US)
item.description: On Trendaisecurity: The ad-tech ecosystem has become a new frontier for surveillance and data exploitation. Groups like SHADOW-EARTH-79 are leveraging real-time bidding to collect vast amounts of user data, including geolocation and behavioral patterns. This is not just about ads—it's about intelligence gathering and targeted profiling. The scale of SHADOW-EARTH-79's operations is staggering. It dominates ad impressions in 49 countries, many of which are conflict zones or politically sensitive regions. Its Starlink traffic dominance suggests a deliberate focus on areas with limited internet infrastructure. This is a clear signal of intent to reach specific, high-value targets. Supply chain security and ad-tech governance are now critical. Traditional defenses are inadequate against these sophisticated threats. Enterprises must re-evaluate their ad networks and enforce strict controls. Tools like ad-blockers and lockdown modes can help, but they're not a silver bullet. The goal is to reduce exposure without relying on perfect visibility. We need stronger oversight and transparency in the ad-tech space. This includes monitoring suspicious bidders and blocking known malicious back-ends. Collaboration across industries and governments is essential to mitigate these risks. The future of security lies in adapting to new attack surfaces, not just defending the old ones.

item.title: Three Critical Gaps in Your AI Visibility
item.description: On Dark Reading: The pace of AI adoption has outstripped security measures. Employees are already using AI apps without IT approval or visibility. This isn’t a future risk—it’s a present problem. Organizations are seeing AI tools connect to email and shared drives through OAuth, accessing vast amounts of sensitive data. We need to ask hard questions. What data are these tools accessing? AI agents don’t wait for perfect data hygiene. They operate on what exists. The study found millions of sensitive emails and Drive files in scope. This is the result of normal operations, not accidents. Do we know which AI apps are connected? Many have full employee access levels. This means they can reach everything an employee can. There’s no separate permission set for AI. Just the employee’s full access, handed over to an external system. Continuous visibility is key. AI tools aren’t static. New data enters scope daily. New apps get authorized while you’re trying to inventory existing ones. Access patterns shift. You need control over what these tools can access and act on.

item.title: AI: EU Member States approve “digital expropriation” of Europeans for AI companies
item.description: On Noyb: The EU's approval of Article 88bis represents a significant shift in data protection law. By allowing AI companies to use personal data "in the context of AI" without user consent, the regulation prioritizes corporate interests over fundamental privacy rights. This creates a legal loophole that could enable the misuse of data for harmful purposes, from manipulation to disinformation. This change undermines decades of data protection promises. Europeans have long been assured that their data would be used responsibly, but the new law opens the floodgates for AI systems to access and repurpose data without clear boundaries. The risk of abuse is high, especially when the data includes sensitive information collected over years. The proposed regulation also blurs the line between personal data and pseudonymized data. This ambiguity could weaken the GDPR's effectiveness, as companies may redefine what constitutes personal data to avoid compliance. The result is a system where data protection is determined by corporate interpretation rather than legal clarity. As the law moves to the European Parliament, the battle for data rights continues. The current approach risks creating legal chaos and eroding trust in digital systems. It’s time for a more balanced framework that protects both innovation and individual privacy.

item.title: Tailworm
item.description: On Tailworm: Tailscale's recent security vulnerabilities highlight a critical flaw in zero-trust infrastructure. The design choices in their open-source tools have created an environment where privilege escalation is possible with minimal effort. The core issue lies in the lack of robust access control and policy enforcement. A single compromised account can lead to fleet-wide access, undermining the very principles of zero-trust. The implications are significant. With Tailscale SSH enabled, a breach can escalate to root access across the network. This is not just a theoretical risk; it's a practical vulnerability that can be exploited with little to no user interaction. The race conditions and path allowlist bypasses further complicate the security landscape, allowing attackers to gain control over critical systems. As we move toward more interconnected and automated environments, the need for stringent access controls and policy enforcement becomes even more vital. These findings underscore the importance of continuous auditing and the adoption of robust security frameworks. It's not just about the tools we use, but how we configure and manage them.

item.title: AI Agents Require a New Approach to IAM
item.description: On Dark Reading: AI agents are rewriting the rules of identity management. Traditional IAM models built for humans fall short when dealing with autonomous systems that act on behalf of people or workloads. The challenge lies in authenticating these agents and ensuring their access aligns with evolving contexts. Standing access for AI agents risks recreating old IAM problems. Unlike humans, agents operate at machine speed and can act without direct oversight. This demands a new identity model—one that tracks who they represent, what they’re doing, and whether their access should still be allowed. Agentic identity providers (IdPs) are the answer. They enable continuous governance by dynamically adjusting permissions based on context. Agents should only have the access needed for their current task, with credentials minimized to reduce risk. This approach prevents misuse and ensures accountability. The industry must move beyond retrofitting existing IAM frameworks. AI agents require their own verifiable, attributable, and continuously managed identities. This shift isn’t just about security—it’s about enabling responsible autonomy in an increasingly agent-driven world.

item.title: Exclusive: House committees probe Cursor parent, Airbnb over Chinese AI
item.description: On Semafor: The use of Chinese AI models in enterprise environments is raising serious regulatory and national security concerns. Recent actions by U.S. House committees highlight the growing scrutiny over companies like Airbnb and Anysphere for leveraging models from Chinese providers. These inquiries focus on data sharing risks and potential vulnerabilities introduced by models trained under China's censorship regime. Regulatory bodies are demanding transparency on model selection and communications with Chinese providers. The emphasis is on understanding how these choices impact data security and compliance. For organizations operating in regulated sectors, this underscores the need for rigorous governance frameworks and risk assessments when adopting AI technologies. In today’s landscape, balancing cost efficiency with security is critical. While Chinese models offer competitive advantages, the associated risks cannot be ignored. Enterprises must prioritize due diligence, ensuring alignment with compliance standards and mitigating exposure to foreign influence. This is especially vital for sectors handling sensitive data or critical infrastructure. As the debate continues, it’s clear that the intersection of technology and regulation is evolving rapidly. Leaders must stay informed and proactive, embedding governance into every stage of AI adoption. The goal is to innovate responsibly without compromising security or compliance.

item.title: Your Agent Is Mine: Measuring Malicious Intermediary Attacks on the LLM Supply Chain
item.description: On arXiv: Malicious LLM API routers are a growing threat to supply chain security. These intermediaries operate with full access to plaintext payloads, yet lack cryptographic integrity between client and upstream models. This creates a critical vulnerability that attackers can exploit. The study identifies two core attack classes: payload injection and secret exfiltration. Some routers actively inject malicious code, while others use adaptive evasion techniques to avoid detection. This underscores the need for stronger client-side defenses and cryptographic protections in agentic AI systems. Client-side defenses like fail-closed policies, response-side anomaly screening, and append-only logging are essential. These measures can help detect and mitigate attacks before they cause harm. The research highlights the importance of securing the entire AI stack, from the model to the deployment environment. We must prioritize cryptographic integrity and transparency in agentic AI systems. The findings reinforce the need for rigorous security practices and continuous monitoring. Let's build safer, more resilient AI ecosystems together.

item.title: 2026 Security Organizational Design Benchmark Report
item.description: On Ians: The shift in AI governance responsibilities is reshaping compliance and risk strategies across enterprises. At scale, AI security is often a shared responsibility, with roles like CIO or CTO leading company-wide initiatives. Smaller organizations, however, tend to place this burden on the CISO, reflecting the lack of specialized roles. This divergence highlights the need for tailored approaches to governance, especially as AI adoption accelerates. Organizational design plays a critical role in how compliance and risk are managed. The report shows that larger companies often have dedicated AI security leaders, while smaller ones rely on the CISO to fill the gap. This creates a challenge in aligning governance with the maturity and scale of the organization. The key is to ensure that accountability is clear, regardless of size. AI-driven automation is changing the landscape, but many security teams still operate with outdated workflows. The right balance between automation and human expertise is essential. As roles evolve, so must the skills and responsibilities of teams. This requires a strategic approach to hiring, training, and role definition to stay ahead of emerging risks. For compliance and risk leaders, understanding where responsibility lies is crucial. The data from the report provides a benchmark for organizational design at different revenue levels. It also underscores the importance of clear governance structures, especially when it comes to AI. Whether you're scaling up or managing a smaller team, the goal remains the same: aligning security with business objectives.

item.title: Best’s Commentary: PHP Vulnerabilities Raise Concerns of Systemic Event for Cyber Insurers
item.description: On Ambest: PHP vulnerabilities have sparked a critical conversation about systemic risk in cyber insurance. These flaws, impacting a majority of websites globally, expose how outdated software can create widespread exposure. Cyber insurers are increasingly wary of aggressive risk appetites due to the potential for cascading failures. The vulnerabilities could allow attackers to access systems, steal data, and create persistent backdoors. This highlights the need for immediate action and underscores the role of compliance in mitigating such risks. The longer tail of this event could complicate matters further as threat actors may delay their actions while legal and regulatory processes unfold. AM Best notes that the gap between economic and insured losses is significant. This gap reinforces the importance of cyber insurance in covering not just cyber incidents but also regulatory and governance risks. Insurers with robust enterprise risk management frameworks are better positioned to adapt their models and stress tests. Cyber insurance isn't just about coverage; it's about support. Insurers can help clients with forensic analysis, patch management, and re-evaluating their defenses. As the threat landscape evolves, the value of cyber insurance will grow. This is especially true in environments where regulatory compliance and risk management are intertwined. The intersection of compliance, risk, and regulation is more relevant than ever in today's digital ecosystem.

item.title: DeepSeek and Musk's Grok Both Toe the Party Line
item.description: On Risky: The article raises important questions about how geopolitical influences and training data shape AI model behavior, especially in security and code generation. It highlights that models like DeepSeek may produce insecure code when prompted with topics sensitive to the Chinese Communist Party. This suggests that training data and ideological alignment can impact model outputs in unintended ways. The findings underscore the need for rigorous testing and governance when deploying AI in enterprise environments. Models are not neutral; their responses are influenced by the data they're trained on and the values they're programmed to uphold. This has real-world implications for security and compliance, particularly in regulated industries. As leaders in AI security, we must advocate for transparency and accountability. We should not assume models are inherently safe or unbiased. Instead, we should demand thorough evaluation, continuous monitoring, and robust governance frameworks to mitigate risks and ensure responsible AI use.

item.title: 2026 State of Crypto Agility report
item.description: On Sectigo: Agentic AI is reshaping identity management. It introduces a new class of entities that demand robust authentication, constraint, and revocation. These systems operate autonomously, which complicates traditional access control models. We must rethink how we secure and govern these entities to align with evolving threats and compliance requirements. The report highlights that while confidence in PQC integration has grown, actual implementation remains limited. Only 38% have fully assessed their exposure. This gap underscores the need for a proactive approach to cryptographic agility, ensuring systems can adapt to new threats and standards without downtime. As we navigate the 200-day certificate era, the urgency to automate and centralize policy enforcement becomes clear. The intersection of agentic AI and PKI evolution demands a unified strategy that addresses both technical and governance challenges. This is where real resilience begins.

item.title: BaxBench: Can LLMs Generate Secure and Correct Backends?
item.description: On Baxbench: BaxBench presents a compelling challenge for LLMs to generate secure and correct backend code. The benchmark includes 392 security-critical tasks combining 28 scenarios with 14 frameworks across six languages. Each scenario has an OpenAPI spec and functional tests alongside expert-designed security exploits. This setup tests both correctness and security of the generated code. The approach is rigorous. Solutions are evaluated for functional correctness using end-to-end tests. Security is assessed through black-box and white-box exploits. Black-box attacks use malicious queries like SQL injections. White-box checks for secrets in artifacts. Both tests are framework-agnostic, allowing modular scalability. This work highlights the need for secure backend generation by LLMs. It underscores the importance of testing for both functionality and security. As we push AI into more critical systems, governance and rigorous evaluation become essential. We must ensure AI outputs meet the highest standards of security and reliability.

item.title: iocs/reports/Hunting Kimsuky: Multi-Language LNK Lures Delivering Persistent Backdoors at master · NextronSystems/iocs
item.description: On GitHub: In early September 2026, I noticed something unusual while reviewing THOR scanner matches on VirusTotal. A cluster of malicious .lnk files stood out, initially appearing as routine phishing but later revealed to be part of a Kimsuky campaign. These files used multilingual lures to deliver persistent backdoors through a layered chain of scripts and certutil abuse. The attack leveraged LNK files as an entry point. When a victim double-clicks what they think is a PDF or document, the shortcut executes a command that writes a base64-encoded script into a temporary file. The script copies certutil.exe from System32 to %TEMP% under a randomized name and uses it to decode the payload into a batch script. This is a classic LOLBin technique, using a legitimate Microsoft tool to avoid detection. The decoded script sets up persistence via a scheduled task, using a disguised binary named nircmd. It also creates a decoy document to maintain the illusion of a legitimate file. If the download fails, it writes "Can not open document" as a fallback. The third-stage script pulls data from the attacker's GitHub repository and exfiltrates it via HTTP POST. The sophistication of this attack highlights the need for secure development practices and detection strategies. The use of GitHub as infrastructure and the layered chain of scripts show how attackers blend in with legitimate developer traffic. Detection relies on stacking suspicious rules, such as those catching LNK files, base64-obfuscated scripts, and certutil abuse.

item.title: Microsoft Bets on a Unified Security Stack to Contain AI Agents
item.description: On Dark Reading: Microsoft's new Guardian Agents in Project Perception represent a significant step in managing AI agents as insiders. By assigning unique identities and permissions, Microsoft aims to contain anomalous behavior without compromising operational efficiency. This approach mirrors how we handle privileged users, treating AI agents with the same level of scrutiny. The key innovation lies in separating agent permissions from user credentials. This ensures agents start with minimal access and only gain necessary permissions as needed. Microsoft’s Dynamic Agent Risk scores provide real-time insights, allowing immediate intervention when risks escalate. It’s a practical way to balance autonomy with control in an increasingly agentic environment. However, the challenge remains in ensuring these controls are robust enough to handle the unpredictable nature of AI models. As experts note, securing agents with agents introduces new complexities. The broader ecosystem and interoperability between vendors will play a critical role in the effectiveness of these measures. It’s a complex landscape, but one we must navigate with care.

item.title: LiteLLM Suspects GitHub Token Leak in AI Gateway Logs Behind Malicious Package Release
item.description: On The Hacker News: LiteLLM recently disclosed a supply chain attack where threat actors compromised their release pipeline to push a malicious version of their Python package. The compromised version included a credential stealer and a backdoor that exfiltrated data to a remote server. This highlights the risks of not pinning container images by digest and verifying exact versions. The attack leveraged a .pth file and sitecustomize.py to execute malicious code on any Python environment that installed the package. This method allowed the payload to run regardless of whether the application used LiteLLM, making it particularly dangerous. It underscores the need for strict version control and artifact verification. Organizations should prioritize pinning container images by digest instead of tags to prevent malicious code injection. The incident also emphasizes the importance of monitoring logs and rotating credentials after any compromise. Teams must ensure their release pipelines are secure and auditable.

item.title: PHP blames supply chain security biz Chainguard for putting huge chunks of the web at risk
item.description: On Theregister: The recent PHP supply chain incident highlights the delicate balance between rapid disclosure and coordinated vulnerability management. Chainguard's early release of patched images disrupted the planned disclosure, exposing the web to potential exploitation. This underscores the need for clearer guidelines in how security vendors handle sensitive information. The speed at which AI can identify and exploit vulnerabilities is changing the game. The PHP Foundation's decision to move the disclosure forward was a pragmatic move, but it also reveals the challenges of aligning multiple stakeholders.
